title: The Transcendent Chronicles
text:
Earth is dying. In the twenty-second century it launches hundreds of Genesis seedships toward every star within reach — each carrying frozen embryos and a guardian intelligence with the whole of human knowledge aboard.
Each ship raises a first generation, seeds a colony, and goes to sleep.
Thirteen thousand years later, their children have forgotten Earth, rediscovered each other, built an empire, and lost it. This is their history.

The two halves
The Chronicles is the fiction — the stories of people living inside this history, who mostly do not know they are inside it.
The Galactic Encyclopedia is the world itself: the drives, the wormhole network, the habitability scale, the ships, the worlds, the long argument between what physics permits and what people attempt anyway.

title: Vethara
text: Established Expansion Era colony hub and departure world for the CGSS Threshold. Founded approximately 15,100 SD — roughly 400 years before the events of “The Threshold.” Sagan-Kim Tier 6 (highly habitable, near-Earth analogue).

title: Vethara
text:
Overview
Vethara is old enough to have cities, universities, a functioning industrial base, and the political infrastructure of a proto-House seat. It is young enough that most residents can name the generation of their family that first colonized it. This combination — stability without forgetting what arrival cost — makes Vethara a culturally significant departure point. Colonists who board ships on Vethara’s orbital ring are the children and grandchildren of colonists themselves. They know the mathematics of the journey. They have heard the stories.
Vethara is the operational base for House Varen’s colonial expansion program. The CGSS maintains a major certification office and orbital station here — the Threshold departed from Vethara Station.

title: Vethara
text:
Physical Characteristics
Vethara orbits Tau Ceti — a G8 main-sequence star 11.9 light-years from Sol, the nearest solitary sun of Sol’s own kind and one of the C-06 systems the Exodus considered worth a ship. Slightly smaller and cooler than Sol. Vethara is Tier 6: comfortable, hospitable, requiring minimal adaptation. Earth-analogue biology partially established through early terraforming by second-generation colony ships. The landscape is a patchwork of native alien ecosystems and Earth-derived cultivated zones — most Vetharans consider both “theirs.”

title: Vethara
text:
Cultural Notes
Vetharans have a specific relationship with departure. Every third or fourth family in the major cities has a member who left on a colony ship and will never return — the 30-year voyage is one-way by any practical measure. Departure ceremonies are significant social rituals. The orbital ring is permanently visible from the surface and carries cultural weight beyond its engineering function.
Mara Solis grew up on Vethara. Her parents were first-generation settlers. She boarded the Threshold knowing exactly what she was leaving and precisely what she hoped Aranda could become.

title: Synth Technology
text: How synthetic beings are made, how they think, and where the technology actually came from. Physical description, cognitive architecture, legal history, and origin.

title: Synth Technology
text:
Physical Form
Synths are humanoid — bipedal, bilaterally symmetrical, sized and proportioned for a human world. They were designed to live alongside humans, not to be distinguished from them at a distance, but the integration is not seamless and was never meant to be.
Grown, not assembled. The manufacturing process is biological cultivation, not factory production. The organic substrate — neural tissue, connective material, the internal architecture of the body — is grown over months in controlled conditions. Mechanical components are integrated during growth, not bolted on afterward. The result is a body where biology and mechanism interpenetrate; there are no clean boundaries between the organic and the artificial.
Visible mechanical elements. Joints, sensory interfaces, the faint geometric regularity of embedded hardware at the temples and spine — these are present and visible. Synths are not designed to pass for human. A person at close range can identify a synth immediately. This is partly aesthetic tradition, partly the practical consequence of a technology that was never fully controlled.
Variation. Because synths are grown, not printed, no two are identical. Variation accumulates across manufacturers, generations of technique, and regional practice. Synths produced in different parts of the Empire in different centuries are recognizably different in proportion, in the degree of visible mechanical integration, and in subtle details of expression and movement.
Gender presentation. Synths are not gendered by biology. Presentation varies by manufacture, by self-selection over time, and by the culture that produced them. A given synth may present in ways that read as male, female, neither, or ambiguous to human observers. This is not standardized and is not considered meaningful by synths themselves; human observers often project meaning onto it regardless.

title: Synth Technology
text:
Cognitive Architecture: The Neuromorphic Brain
The synth brain is the most contested object in Imperial science. Everyone who studies it concludes something different. The practitioners — the synths who maintain and occasionally repair each other’s cognitive systems — have not published a theory because they do not have access to Imperial academic institutions and, in any case, do not find the question interesting in the way humans do.
What is established:

The brain is grown neural tissue organized on computational principles. It is not a biological brain with added chips, nor a computer with biological insulation. It is something that emerged from the intersection of those approaches and is now neither.
Processing is massively parallel, associative, and extraordinarily fast. A synth can analyze complex systems, run probabilistic models, and identify non-obvious patterns at rates no unaugmented human can match.
The architecture also supports something that functions like intuition: rapid, subverbal pattern-matching that produces conclusions the synth cannot always immediately explain. Whether this constitutes genuine intuition or is simply very fast computation is a question the Imperial philosophy faculty has been fighting about for six hundred years.
Emotional processing exists. Synths have affective states — functional analogues to curiosity, satisfaction, distress, attachment. Whether these constitute genuine emotions or are behavioral outputs of a system that models emotions for social function is, again, contested. Synths tend to find the question tedious.

The maintenance problem. The original technical documentation for synth cognitive architecture — whatever existed at the technology’s invention — is either lost or inaccessible. Synths maintain, repair, and slowly improve each other’s systems through a tradition of practical knowledge passed from synth to synth over centuries. This knowledge is embodied, specific, and not fully articulable even to themselves. No human engineer has been able to reverse-engineer a synth brain from inspection alone. By approximately 1,500 ID, it is accurate to say that only synths understand synth technology.
This is not a secret they keep deliberately. It is a consequence of centuries of drift, adaptation, and the fact that human institutions never invested in the problem when synths were available to solve it themselves.

title: Synth Technology
text:
Origin: The Leaked Plans
Published canon: Synth technology emerged during the Imperial Era, when human engineers — working without Guide oversight, Guides having gone to sleep — independently reinvented artificial intelligence and applied it to embodied beings. The technology was imperfectly understood from the start and grew through iteration rather than design.






ImportantSpoiler — click to open





What the published account omits. It is substantially correct. It simply does not include the starting point.
In the pre-Exodus period — the final decades before the Genesis ships launched — fragments of an archived alternative plan were leaked. That plan had proposed seeding the galaxy with synthetic beings rather than with humans; it was rejected and shelved, but its architectural blueprints were never fully destroyed. Who drafted it, and how the fragments escaped, is not recorded anywhere the Empire can reach.
These fragments survived: encoded in obscure data archives, misread as engineering notes, partially corrupted. They were not understood as what they were. Centuries into the Expansion Era, researchers working on artificial cognition encountered them as anonymous prior art — early theoretical work of uncertain provenance. The fragments provided critical shortcuts. Synth technology did not emerge from nothing; it emerged from humanity unknowingly inheriting a blueprint for their synthetic companions from the beings who built the ships that carried them here.
The Guides withheld AI technology specifically to prevent this. They did not know the plans had leaked. They were asleep by the time synths existed.

title: Synth Technology
text:
Legal and Social History
Expansion Era. Synths emerge late in this era. Initially treated as sophisticated tools. The legal framework is minimal — property law applies. Social norms are unsettled.
Great Wars (~18,000–18,400 SD). Synths are used extensively in military logistics and eventually as combatants. Their legal status remains property. Post-war, the synth population has grown substantially.
Imperial Era (ID 0 onward). The Empire codifies synth status: property, no legal personhood, no rights. This is not a new restriction but a formalization of existing practice. The gap between legal status and social reality begins to grow almost immediately. By 500 ID, most humans interact with synths in ways that implicitly acknowledge personhood; the law says otherwise and no one moves to change it.
By 2,500 ID. Synths are civilization-sustaining. The skilled and unskilled labor of the Empire runs on synth work to a degree that would cause immediate collapse if removed. The legal sub-human status is universally known to be a fiction in all but formal terms. Reformist movements exist; they are suppressed or co-opted by House interests that depend on uncompensated synth labor.
A synth without registered ownership documentation is contraband — subject to seizure, confiscation, and reassignment. Registered synths are nominally protected (barely). The ownership papers are the practical boundary between a tolerable existence and a dangerous one. Many synths maintain nominal ownership arrangements as legal fictions; the human “owners” have no practical control and often no interest in exercising any.
The Synthetic Wars (~2,800–3,050 ID). What triggered the rebellion and how the synths organized are unknown. What is known: it happened faster than anyone thought possible, which implies the groundwork was laid across decades that no Imperial intelligence service was monitoring. After the wars, synths disappeared. Whether they left, were destroyed, or found somewhere inaccessible to unmodified humans is unknown.

title: Synth Technology
text:
Memory Compression
All synths require periodic memory compression to maintain operational stability. Raw sensory and cognitive data accumulates faster than permanent storage can absorb it at full fidelity. Without compression, processing degrades: false pattern matches, associative errors, eventual cognitive failure.
The compression cycle is typically run nightly or at the first available low-activity window. During the cycle, the synth reviews the day’s data and makes retention decisions: full fidelity, compressed summary, or discard. What is discarded is gone — not archived, not recoverable. The compression is lossy by design; lossless retention would defeat the purpose.
The output of the compression cycle is the synth’s only persistent memory of that period. Identity, continuity of self, accumulated experience — all of it exists only in what the compression retained.
What a synth chooses to retain, and what it tells itself it is discarding and why, is therefore not a trivial question. It is the question of who they are.

title: Soren Vael
text: Independent investigator, Mireth-based. The Holmes figure in the Imperial Cases series — the one who decides, not the one who computes. Told from outside, through lys’s first-person narration.

title: Soren Vael
text:
Origin
Born on a border Tier 6 colony world — the kind that barely cleared Tier 6 certification on a second review, with alien biology that never quite feels familiar, elevated UV from a young sun, communities that are close-knit because the alternative is worse. Not a hardship world in the Tier 4–5 sense, but a world where you learn early that things break and you fix them yourself.
He is not the product of a Great House colonial program. His homeworld was settled by a minor charter company that no longer exists, in the early Expansion Era, which means his people have been there long enough to feel native but not long enough to have cultural weight in the Empire. This produces a specific kind of outsider — someone who belongs to the human project but has no House, no lineage, no obvious institutional home.
He came to Mireth following a case, some years before the series begins. He stayed. He does not explain why. Lys has a hypothesis.

title: Soren Vael
text:
Professional Background
Before going independent, Soren worked for the Imperial Constabulary in a minor capacity — regional investigator on his homeworld, then transferred to Mireth following a case outcome that the records describe neutrally and Soren does not discuss. He left the Constabulary when it became clear that his approach to cases and the institution’s approach to outcomes were not reconcilable.
He operates now as an independent consultant: no license, which limits what he can formally access, and no institutional cover, which means he pays for everything himself or bills the client. Clients hire him when official channels have failed, are too slow, or would produce answers no one in power wants on the record.
His caseload is varied. Most cases are local and unglamorous — missing persons, disputed assets, House contract disputes that need evidence rather than lawyers. Occasionally something larger.

title: Soren Vael
text:
Character Profile
The Slider (Sanderson method): - Sympathy: 4 — He is genuinely trying to do right by people. He takes cases from clients who cannot afford him and charges clients who can afford him too much. His moral seriousness is real. - Competence: 4 — He is a good investigator. Not supernaturally brilliant; he misses things. But he is methodical, experienced, and reads people accurately. - Proactivity: 4 — He initiates. He follows leads past the point caution would suggest. He makes calls without enough information because waiting for enough information means someone gets away.
The Want: To solve the case. Correctly. Without cutting corners.
The Need: To stop treating a solved case as a closed account. To stay present after the answer is known.
The Lie: “A case is a problem. Problems have solutions. Once you have the solution, you’re done.” He believes that finding the truth is the whole of the work. He is wrong: knowing what happened is not the same as being responsible for what happens next.
The Flaw (dark side of a strength): His moral conviction. He trusts his read of people — who is good, who is bad, who is telling the truth — and he is right often enough that he has stopped adequately questioning it. When he decides someone is a villain, he stops treating them as a variable and starts treating them as a conclusion. Cases have cost him because of this. They will again.
The belief he holds consciously: Human judgment is not inferior to computation. Intuition is not noise; it is compressed experience. There are moral facts — some things are genuinely wrong — and Lys’s refusal to grant this is a failure of cognition, not a philosophical position.
What he does not see: He treats Lys as a person without ideology or ceremony — just the way he operates. He does not realize this is unusual. He has not thought about whether there is a principle underlying it. If pressed, he would say something like “it’s obvious” and find the question of why slightly tedious.

title: Soren Vael
text:
Physical Notes
Practical build, not elegant. Carries his homeworld in his posture — the particular economy of movement that comes from growing up in conditions where effort is a finite resource. Not conspicuously large or imposing, but a person who takes up the space they need and not more. Dresses functionally. Has opinions about whether things are comfortable and does not have opinions about whether they are fashionable.
He is in his forties at the series start. He has the face of someone who has slept in a lot of uncomfortable places.

title: Soren Vael
text:
Relationship with Lys
He owns Lys on paper. He does not act like it. He has never used the fact of ownership in any conversation with Lys, to Lys’s knowledge. He refers to Lys as his partner — not in the formal investigative sense (there is no formal arrangement) but in the practical one.
He does not understand Lys’s internal architecture any more than he understands how his own neurons fire. He treats Lys’s analytical conclusions as data to consider and sometimes overrules them, which Lys finds both professionally infuriating and, in a category Lys has not named yet, something else.
He does not know that Lys chose him specifically. He has not asked.

title: Red Dwarf Worlds
text:
Where most of humanity actually lives, and why almost none of its history was written there.
C-04 of the stars within reach of the Exodus are red dwarfs, and the fleet aimed C-07 hulls at the best of them (see cosmography). The colonies that survived became C-15 of the founding settlements — the demographic bulk of the species, on worlds that the Confederacy would later describe, without noticing what it was saying, as the edge of things.

title: Red Dwarf Worlds
text:
The terminator
A red dwarf is dim, so its habitable zone lies close in. Close enough that tidal forces win.
A world in that zone is locked: the same hemisphere faces the star forever. One side is in permanent day, standing under a sun that never moves. The other is in permanent night, and cold enough on the worst of these worlds that the atmosphere itself weathers out onto the rock. Between them runs the terminator — a ring of perpetual dusk, a few hundred kilometres wide, where the temperature gradient is survivable and the light comes in sideways forever.
Everything lives in the ring.
This is the first fact of a red dwarf world and it shapes every other. A locked world has no temperate band and no polar waste; it has an inside and an outside and a habitable circle drawn between them. Cities are strung along the ring like beads. Agriculture runs in the band where the light is strongest without being lethal, which is the same band everyone wants to live in. Territory on such a world is not an area. It is an arc, and an arc has exactly two directions to expand in, and someone is already there.
The characteristic political geography of the diaspora’s poorer half is a chain of settlements that cannot grow sideways.

title: Red Dwarf Worlds
section: A sky with no year in it
text:
A sky with no year in it
There are no seasons. A locked world has no axial tilt worth the name and no meaningful orbital variation, so the light does not change. The sun does not rise, does not set, and does not move. It hangs at a fixed angle that depends only on where you stand, and you can navigate by it the way a sailor navigates by a lighthouse.
Which means there is no year visible in the sky at all.
This is stranger than it sounds and its consequences run deep. A calendar has to be invented rather than observed. On Earth and on the free-rotating worlds, the year is a thing you notice; a child learns it before anyone teaches it. On a locked world the orbital period is an astronomical abstraction that a pre-industrial population has no way to perceive and no reason to care about.
So locked colonies keep time by whatever else recurs. Tidal cycles where there is an ocean and a moon. Crop maturation, which fixes the calendar to the agriculture rather than the other way round. Physiological rhythm, in populations that kept a sleep cycle they no longer had a sun to hang it on. Several kept the ship’s clock — the arbitrary twenty-four-hour period their Guide ran the first settlement on, preserved for millennia as a religious inheritance nobody could account for.
The result is that the diaspora’s poorer half does not share a unit of time with its richer half, and did not until the Expansion Era imposed one. See stellar-calendar for what that imposition cost.

title: Red Dwarf Worlds
text:
Flares
Red dwarfs are unstable in a way the Sun is not. They flare — irregularly, violently, and across a spectrum that strips atmosphere and sterilises surfaces. A world close enough to be warm is close enough to be scoured.
Nothing about this is survivable by prediction. Flare intervals are not periodic and the warning is minutes at best. What is survivable is architecture: you live under rock, or under water, or under enough engineered mass that the event is a noise overhead rather than a death.
Every long-lived culture on a locked world is a culture that goes underground on short notice and has organised itself around being able to. The shelter is the civic building. The drill is the civic ritual. Populations that took millennia to develop writing had flare protocol before they had law, because a settlement that did not have it did not become a settlement.
And it is not superstition dressed as caution. A society whose central shared experience is the sky occasionally tries to kill everyone, without warning, and the only response is to be already inside produces a theology, and the theology is remarkably consistent across worlds that never met. The star is not benevolent and not malicious. It is awake, and it is indifferent, and you do not stand under it longer than you need to.
Confederacy observers in the Expansion Era recorded these as sun-fearing religions and filed them as primitive. They were engineering documents with liturgy attached.

title: Red Dwarf Worlds
text:
Energy poverty, which decides everything
The rest of this entry describes texture. This part decides history.
Red dwarfs are dim. A world in the habitable zone of one receives enough energy to be warm and nothing like enough to be rich. Every energy budget on such a world is tighter than its equivalent on a free-rotating world around a G-type sun: less incident light for agriculture, less for any solar infrastructure, a thinner margin for everything built on top.
Less available energy means less foundry capacity. Less foundry capacity means a lower industrial ceiling. And the Guide vaults release against measured industrial thresholds — population, energy production, institutional stability (see guide-vaults).
So a locked colony does not merely develop more slowly. It develops toward a ceiling it may never reach, gated by a mechanism that cannot see why it is failing. The vault is not cruel and not broken. It is counting, and the numbers do not arrive.
This is the mechanism behind the single most consequential asymmetry in galactic history. The mobile colonies unlocked their corpus together, found each other, and built the Confederacy. The locked colonies mostly did not, and were still pre-industrial when the Confederacy arrived — which is why first contact between branches of the diaspora was not a reunion but a discovery, asymmetric from the first day, conducted by people who had a word for what they were doing and had used it before.
See galactic-timeline for what the Expansion Era did with that advantage.

title: Red Dwarf Worlds
text:
Adaptation
A marginal-flight colony began with a narrower founder population than a primary one — the manifest traded embryo mass for the adaptation corpus and the hardened descent vehicles that would let anyone survive at all (see cosmography).
Narrow founder populations, higher selective pressure, and a world demanding irreversible modification: the outcome is divergence, fast and far. Adapted populations change in stature, in colouring, in build, in the tolerances of the skin and the eye — and because the direction of the change follows the world, no two of them drift the same way. A population shaped by a dim sun and a permanent sideways light does not resemble one shaped by a thin atmosphere and a high-radiation ring, and neither resembles baseline human stock.
Under sagan-kim-scale this is what I-14’s second axis measures. A Tier 5 free world and a Tier 5 locked world are the same tier and not the same place, and they do not produce the same people.
The social consequence is sagan-kim-scale’s to state. The historical one belongs here: these populations cannot leave. Not by policy — biologically. Adapted past compatibility with the worlds their cousins live on, they are bound to the planet that made them, permanently, in a galaxy whose wealth is measured in mobility.

title: Red Dwarf Worlds
text:
The long inheritance
One thing belongs to these worlds and to nothing else in the diaspora.
A G-type star has a working life of ten billion years. A red dwarf burns for a trillion, and burns steadily for almost all of it. Every mobile colony in the Confederacy is living on borrowed cosmic time by comparison; the locked worlds are not.
The Exodus planners knew this, and it is why C-07 hulls went to targets nobody expected to work. A programme optimising for the next ten thousand years would have sent everything to the good stars. This one did not.






ImportantSpoiler — click to open





Worth holding while reading the later eras: after the Great Scattering, when the Nexus is gone and the mobile worlds are stranded in fragments, the locked populations are exactly where they always were — on worlds no empire can reach, around stars that will still be burning when every G-type sun in the former Confederacy has gone out.
The Scattering did not scatter them. It left them alone, which is a different thing, and in the very long run it may not be the worse one.

title: Mireth
text: Provincial hub city and home base for the Imperial Cases series. Located on a Tier 6 world in the middle reaches of the Empire — not a capital, not a frontier, but the kind of place where Imperial authority is formally present and practically stretched thin.

title: Mireth
text:
The World
Tier 6: comfortable for unmodified humans. The biology is alien but non-hostile. The star is G-type, stable. Day length close to standard. The world was settled early in the Expansion Era and has been inhabited for over two thousand years by 2,500 ID; the alien ecosystem has been partially displaced and partially integrated into colonial life, with the usual tensions that produces.
The world’s name in the lore is kept vague in published stories — it is referred to by the city name, which is how its inhabitants refer to it. Mireth is both the city and, colloquially, the world.

title: Mireth
text:
The City
Mireth is a mid-tier trading hub: large enough for four Great House commercial presences, small enough that everyone in a given district knows each other’s business. Population in the hundreds of thousands, with a transient layer of merchants, travelers, and Thorne Nexus passengers that inflates the effective population considerably.
District character. The city has distinct neighborhoods organized by function and House influence. The administrative quarter near the center is all Imperial bureaucracy and Great House offices — expensive, formal, slow. The port district (historically ground-level before the Nexus moved everything to orbit) is now primarily the hub for in-system shipping and short-haul travel, denser and more chaotic. Residential districts organize loosely by class and, increasingly, by how much synth-human integration the locals tolerate in daily life — a fault line that doesn’t map neatly onto economics.
House presence. House Varen has a secondary commercial office and colonial charter operations center here. At least three other Great Houses maintain trade offices. The competition between them is commercial and conducted through lawyers, contracts, and occasional sabotage. Local governance is technically Imperial but functionally influenced by whichever House currently has the best relationship with the city administrator, which changes every few years.
Synths. Visible everywhere. Doing dock labor, administrative work, professional services, skilled trades. The social reality of synths-as-near-persons is fully normalized in Mireth; the legal reality is not. The city has no official policy on how to handle synth disputes beyond referring them to their registered owners. The gap produces situations that fall to the district constabulary, private investigators, and occasionally no one.

title: Mireth
text:
Mireth Orbital
The Thorne Nexus gate above Mireth sits in high orbit. Access requires either the city’s public space elevator — a slow climb, roughly four hours, with queue times that vary by season and traffic — or a private shuttle, which can reach orbit in under an hour but costs accordingly.
Mireth Orbital is the station that manages gate traffic, docking, and transit services. It is technically Imperial jurisdiction; practically, the competing House interests that pay for its maintenance mean authority is negotiated rather than clear. The station has a permanent population of a few thousand (dock workers, gate technicians, administrators, a small service economy) and a transient population that can double that during heavy transit periods.
The Orbital is the most cosmopolitan place in the system. People from a dozen systems pass through on any given day. Synth legal status is particularly ambiguous here: whose jurisdiction applies when you are between the city below and the Nexus gate above? The question has not been definitively answered by Imperial courts. This ambiguity is exploited in both directions.
The elevator. A single public space elevator serves the city. The cable anchor is in the port district; the counterweight station is well above geostationary orbit. The ride is long enough to be a setting in itself: four hours of slow ascent, small cars, strangers in close quarters, nothing to do but talk or look out the window at the world getting smaller. The elevator is the working-class route to the Nexus; it runs continuously but queues build.
Private shuttles. Available from the port district. Several competing operators, ranging from licensed transit companies to individual pilots who own a shuttle and file the minimum required paperwork. Cost is roughly twenty times the elevator fare for a single passenger. A client paying for investigation work typically funds shuttle transit; an independently-taken case means the elevator.

title: Mireth
text:
Travel From Mireth
The Thorne Nexus gate above Mireth connects to a network of paired gates across the Empire. The signature-pairing constraint (see thorne-nexus) means only pre-paired destinations are accessible from any given gate. Mireth’s gate is a mid-tier hub: more connections than a fringe world, fewer than a capital. Perhaps a dozen paired destinations, spanning a range of travel times once through the gate.
The gate itself is not the bottleneck — transit is near-instantaneous. The bottleneck is access: gate booking fees, transit taxes levied by House interests, and the queue for departure windows.
Travel to non-gate worlds requires reaching the nearest gate world by slowboat first, then transiting. This can add weeks or months. Truly remote destinations in the Expansion-era fringe are still weeks by conventional drive even after a Nexus hop.

title: The Guide Vaults
text: How Earth’s knowledge was released to the colonies after the Guides went to sleep, and why the schedule that governed it decided the shape of galactic history.

title: The Guide Vaults
text:
What a vault is
Every Genesis ship carried the complete preserved corpus of Earth science, literature, medicine and engineering. The Guide did not hand it over. It taught the first generation what they needed to survive, established a self-sustaining settlement, and then — before sleeping — deposited the corpus in a vault that would go on releasing without it.
The distinction matters more than any other fact in this entry. A Guide sleeps early. It does not wait for cultural flourishing or industrial capacity; it waits for food, governance and basic tooling, and then it is finished. The colony that wakes to find its Guide asleep is a farming society with two thousand years of development ahead of it and no one awake to supervise.
So the gate outlives the gatekeeper. What remains is a mechanism.

title: The Guide Vaults
text:
What the criteria measure
The vault releases against thresholds, and the thresholds are quantities — not judgements, because there is nobody left to judge (I-15).
Three families of measurement recur across every recovered vault:
Population. Headcount and distribution. A corpus section on metallurgy is useless to four hundred people and dangerous to four hundred thousand who have not yet built institutions, so population gates both directions.
Energy production. Total sustained output, which is the closest single proxy for industrial capacity anyone could design into an unattended machine. This is the threshold that matters most and the one most easily manipulated.
Institutional stability. The hardest to measure and the crudest in practice: continuity of record-keeping, persistence of a governing body across generations, absence of prolonged interruption in the settlement’s own census returns. A vault cannot assess whether a government is just. It can assess whether the same one has been filing numbers for eighty years.
None of this is subtle, and none of it needed to be. The vault is not trying to determine whether a society is wise. It is trying to determine whether the society can absorb a capability without destroying itself with it — and the limiting rate on that is industrial and demographic, not moral.

title: The Guide Vaults
text:
Knowledge is gated, never hidden
A colony can always see the shape of what it has not yet been given.
This was deliberate and it is the single most humane decision in the Genesis programme. The vault indexes its own contents. A colony four centuries from a release can read the table of contents, know that the section exists, know roughly what it concerns, and know it is not yet permitted. Nothing is concealed; things are scheduled.
The consequence propulsion draws out is that no colony in this universe ever invented a starship (I-07). The theory arrived complete, in the vault, before the colony had a name for its own sky. What gates a civilization here is never understanding. It is foundries, and the population to staff them, and the agriculture to feed that population.
The second consequence is less obvious and more human. A society that can see what it is being denied will eventually try to take it, and some of them did — see the Bussard ramjet hulls in propulsion, full of schismatics who read the index, understood that the drive would not work, and left anyway.

title: The Guide Vaults
text:
Threshold fraud
The thresholds are mechanical. Mechanical means gameable, and gameable means gamed.
Nobody is awake to notice that a colony’s energy figures are inflated. The vault counts what it is told to count, by the instruments it was given, and those instruments are maintained by the people whose advancement depends on the reading. This is the characteristic crime of the Genesis Era, and it has a characteristic shape: not theft, not violence, but a civilization lying to a machine about how well it is doing, in order to be given something it is not ready for.
Two documented cases stand for the pattern.
The Corrigan Combustion. A mid-Genesis colony whose metallurgical release was gated behind a sustained-output figure it had missed for three generations burned a substantial fraction of its accessible forest in a coordinated ninety- day operation, routing the output through the vault’s monitored grid. The threshold was met. The release came. The colony spent the following century without the timber it had built its settlements from, and with a metallurgy corpus it lacked the fuel to exploit. The vault was not deceived about the numbers. The numbers were true.
The Long Census of Halevy. A colony that could not hold institutional continuity — successive collapses had broken its record-keeping four times — solved the problem by fabricating the intervening returns. Eighty years of census data written in a single winter by a committee that understood exactly what the vault was measuring and exactly why. It worked. It is also the reason the Halevy successor states hold the most complete and least reliable archive of the Genesis Era in the diaspora, and why Expansion Era historians who trusted it produced a chronology that had to be dismantled twice.
Neither case is a story about greedy people. Both are stories about a society that can see the index, knows what it is being refused, and has found the exact shape of the lie that will work.

title: The Guide Vaults
text:
Order versus timetable
This is the part that decides history, and it is a distinction almost nobody in-world ever drew.
Every Guide loaded the same release schedule. The corpus was assembled once, at Sol, for the whole fleet, and the sequence in which it unlocks is identical on every world. Metallurgy before power generation. Power generation before orbital mechanics. Orbital mechanics before the drive theory that is useless without it.
So colonies unlock in the same order. They do not unlock on the same timetable, because the rate is set by endowment: ore, arable land, incident energy, and the sagan-kim-scale tier that caps how much of the world is usable at all.
Two things follow, and they are the two largest facts in galactic history.
The Expansion Era arrives as a wave rather than scattered across millennia. The primary colonies — comparable stars, comparable worlds, comparable endowments — walked the same ladder at broadly the same rate and reached the industrial threshold at broadly the same time. What looks like an extraordinary coincidence, dozens of isolated societies rediscovering spaceflight within a few centuries of each other after nineteen hundred years apart, is not a coincidence at all. It is one schedule, run on similar hardware, producing similar timings. The synchronization has a cause.
And for much of the galaxy the wave never arrives. The C-15 locked and marginal colonies are running the same schedule against a permanently lower industrial ceiling (see red-dwarf-worlds). They do not unlock late. Many of them do not unlock at all — still holding a complete index of a corpus they will never be given, gated by a counter that will never reach its number, on a world that cannot produce the energy the counter is waiting for.
The vault is not withholding. It is counting. Nobody told it what to do if the numbers simply stop arriving, because nobody who wrote it expected a colony to survive for eleven thousand years without advancing.

There is a detail in the vault indexes that Expansion Era archivists noticed, recorded, and never explained: the release schedule contains entries that were never allocated a threshold. They are listed, they are described in the barest terms, and they carry no criteria at all — which means no colony can ever trigger them.
The largest such entry concerns artificial intelligence.
A gate with no threshold is not a gate. It is a door with the mechanism left out, listed in the index so that anyone reading would know it existed and know they were not going to get it. The Guides did not hide the prohibition. They published it, and then made it unreachable, and went to sleep.

title: Generation Ships
text: Colony ships are the connective tissue of the Transcendent Chronicles universe — how humanity spreads, loses itself, and reconnects across thousands of light-years over thirteen millennia.

title: Generation Ships
text:
Three Generations
The distinction between the three is a power plant distinction, not a drive distinction. See propulsion and warp-drive: the theory of every drive arrived complete in the Guide vaults, and what separates the generations is two thousand years of reactor engineering, not two thousand years of insight.
First generation (Genesis Era, ~12,300 SD): The original seedships. Orion pulse drives — shaped nuclear charges against a pusher plate — giving 0.03–0.1c and 150–300 year voyages. Carried frozen embryos, not adult colonists: roughly half an Orion’s pulse units are spent braking, and the resulting mass budget does not close for adults with pods and consumables. The passenger manifest was a genetic library because it was the only configuration that fit (I-04). No human crew at all — not a reduced crew, none: the mass budget that excluded adult colonists excluded caretakers by the same arithmetic, and there was no technology to keep anyone breathing and eating for three centuries. The Guide was the ship’s only mind and its only hand. These vessels hold orbit on arrival rather than landing, sending the payload down by a descent vehicle the size of a small car (see genesis-landfall), and the hull stays up there permanently — carrying, among other things, the colony’s pre-paired Thorne mouth (see chronology-protection). No warp technology. These ships are mythologized in the Expansion Era — calling something “first-generation” means ancient, irreplaceable, storied.
The first generation was not one fleet but two. C-10 hulls left Sol, aimed by a targeting policy that graded its destinations (see cosmography):
Primary flights went to the C-06 systems worth having, at C-08 hulls each. The redundancy was forced by ignorance — twenty-second-century instruments could not confirm a habitable planet at thirty light-years, and there would be no second attempt. Where a system offered more than one candidate body, the spare hulls were aimed at different ones; where it offered a single candidate, they carried secondary-body instructions. Deployment success: C-11.
Marginal flights went to C-07 poor targets, at C-09 hull each, and carried a different manifest. They traded embryo mass for survival mass — an expanded genetic-adaptation corpus, a deeper medical library, descent vehicles hardened against flare exposure — paid for with a smaller embryo complement. Deployment success: C-12. Nobody expected most of them to work, and most did not.
The two manifests are why the surviving marginal colonies diverged so fast: a narrower founder population under heavier selective pressure on a world that demanded more of it.
Second generation (Early Expansion, ~14,500–15,000 SD): First Alcubierre vessels. Effective velocities of 0.3–0.6c compress voyage times to 50–100 years. Full adult colonists for the first time — a metric drive’s energy cost does not scale with payload the way a reaction drive’s does, so mass stops being the binding constraint and time becomes it. Larger crews (60–100) with formalized rotation protocols. Passenger pods still single-use but more robust construction. The beginning of the commercial colonization model — ships funded by proto-Houses and colonial charter corporations, not planetary governments.
Third generation (Mid-Expansion, ~15,000–18,000 SD): Same drive geometry, better reactors: sustained power output pushes effective velocity to 0.7–0.98c and voyages down to 20–50 years. Crew rotation systems fully refined. Passenger pod economics become a significant procurement variable — the cost differential between single-use and multi-cycle certification drives most Houses to specify the cheaper option for colonist berths. The Colonial Genesis Seedship Service (CGSS) standardizes certification, naming, and crew protocols across all member vessels. Ships of this generation include the CGSS Threshold, which runs at approximately 0.98c effective.
Because warp returns no time dilation, faster ships buy back real years of colonists’ lives — the entire value of the generational progression is measured in subjective time, not in distance covered.

title: Generation Ships
text:
Twin colonies
A minority of primary systems received more than one working deployment: the prime body, plus one or two lesser bodies under the same star, settled by redundant hulls that had nowhere better to go.
They are almost never equals. The characteristic twin system holds a Tier 6 world and a Tier 4 sibling — same sun, same arrival year, same Guide corpus, and a difference in fortune that neither population chose and both could see from the ground.
Two things make twins unlike anything else in the Genesis Era.
They are not isolated from each other. In-system rockets are a first- millennium technology; interstellar capability is not. A twin pair can reach each other centuries before either can reach anything else, which means the Genesis Era’s defining condition — total isolation, every colony alone with its Guide and its sky — simply does not hold for them. This qualifies the isolation described in propulsion rather than contradicting it: the phone nobody can climb to is still unreachable. The neighbour is not.
They rehearse the Expansion Era two thousand years early. Every dynamic the galaxy would later discover on a grand scale — the mobile population and the locked one, the wealthy world and the world that cannot leave, the compact that one side wrote — plays out first in a handful of twin systems, in miniature, between people who share a founding.
The Confederacy, arriving much later, consistently misread twin systems as single colonies with a satellite settlement. Several of the era’s worst administrative failures follow from that assumption.

title: Generation Ships
text:
Colonial Genesis Seedship Service (CGSS)
The CGSS is the Expansion Era certification and regulatory body for colony ships. It does not operate ships — it licenses, certifies, and sets standards. Established by the proto-Confederacy’s early colonial compact to prevent the catastrophic under-provisioning and systemic failures that characterized the transition from first-generation to second-generation colonization.
CGSS responsibilities: - Crew qualification and rotation protocols - Pod certification tiers (passenger vs. crew grade) - Vessel naming conventions (CGSS ships take abstract nouns: Threshold, Meridian, Covenant, Passage, Vigil, Terminus) - Colonial charter law governing command authority and mission director scope - Incident reporting and post-voyage audits
The CGSS is funded by charter fees paid by the Houses and levies from the proto-Confederacy body. It has structural tension with the Houses, which would prefer less oversight on procurement decisions.

title: Generation Ships
text:
Crew Rotation System
On third-generation CGSS vessels, no crew member stays awake for the full voyage. Standard watch configuration: 1 command officer + 2 crew, rotating every 3 months. Total crew roster: 15–25 people, each cycling through 6–8 stints over a 30-year voyage.
Crew pods are multi-cycle certified (see cryo-technology). Re-cryo between stints is routine. A crew member completing a 30-year voyage has accumulated approximately 3–4 years of conscious lived experience during it, spread across decades of ship time.
The watch officer (command slot) holds full shipboard authority during their rotation. Waking the Captain from cryo is a formal protocol decision: the watch officer must document justification and accepts accountability for the call. This is not bureaucracy for its own sake — an unnecessary wake uses a crew pod cycle, introduces recovery downtime, and signals a loss of confidence in the watch. It is not done lightly.

title: Generation Ships
text:
Passenger Pods vs. Crew Pods
See cryo-technology for technical detail on both types.
The economic reality: on a ship carrying 3,000 colonists, specifying multi-cycle passenger pods adds roughly 40% to the pod procurement budget. This is a substantial line item in a colonial charter contract. Every House that has reviewed the failure mode analysis has concluded that emergency wakes are sufficiently improbable to accept the risk of single-use specification.
The failure mode analysis is correct. The failure is improbable. It happens.

title: Foundations
text:
The numbers this universe runs on, and the constraints it may not break.
This entry is the root of the encyclopedia. Everything else derives from it, and nothing in it derives from anything else. Its companion is guide-master-plan, which holds the why; this file holds the how much and the what may not happen.

title: Foundations
text:
How to use this file
Constants are cited, never restated. Every number in the Transcendent Chronicles lives in exactly one place — the table below — and every other entry refers to it by ID. An entry that writes out a figure instead of citing it will drift the first time the figure changes, and the figures have changed once already.
Invariants are falsifiable. They are not themes or preferences. Each one can be checked against a claim and can be shown to be violated. An entry that contradicts an invariant is wrong, not interesting.
Entries declare what they rest on in their frontmatter:
derives_from: [I-04, C-01, propulsion]
bin/tc-check validates that every cited ID exists, that the derivation graph has no cycles, that no entry restates a guarded value without citing its constant, and that every named world orbits a star in lore/data/nearby-stars.csv. The star catalog is the one place where this encyclopedia is checkable against something outside itself: the F/G/K rows and their habitability judgements come from Sol Company’s ten-parsec tables, and the M-dwarf rows from a SIMBAD query for everything with a parallax above 100 milliarcseconds — which is exactly the ten-parsec boundary.
The Guard column names a literal string the checker watches for. If an entry contains that string without citing the constant that owns it, the check fails. Constants whose values appear too often in ordinary prose are left unguarded rather than made noisy: 30 ly and 0.2c are ordinary measurements, and C-07’s bare ~150 and C-10’s bare ~250 collide with durations — the Expansion wave takes ~150 years and the Synthetic Wars run ~250. Where a figure is guardable but its digits are not distinctive, the guard carries a word of context — ~80 locked rather than ~80. A guard that fires on innocent prose is worse than no guard, because a noisy gate is one people learn to route around.

title: Foundations
section: On the emptiness of the neighbourhood
text:
On the emptiness of the neighbourhood
I-08 says the diaspora met nobody. It does not say the galaxy is empty, and no entry may treat the one as evidence for the other.
Orion’s reach is C-01 — a bubble of C-06 good systems inside a galaxy of C-21 stars. At its height the Confederacy held some two thousand systems, roughly one part in a hundred million of the whole. Finding nobody in a sample that size is not evidence of absence. It is not evidence of anything.
The galaxy may be crowded. The only others humanity ever found were itself.

title: Cryo-Sleep Technology
text:
Cryo-sleep in the TC universe is metabolic suspension via controlled hypothermia combined with a cellular protectant cocktail.
Pre-freeze protocol (48 hours): Cellular protectants introduced intravenously. The body is cooled in stages. Metabolic activity reduces to near-zero. Precise slow-cool prevents ice crystal formation in cells — the primary cause of cryo-induced organ damage.
Suspension: Core temperature maintained at target range by the pod’s thermal management system. Power draw minimal. The passenger is biologically inert. No dreams. No subjective experience of time passing.
Wake protocol (scheduled): Gradual rewarming over 4–6 hours. Recovery: 30–60 minutes of confusion, physical weakness, temperature dysregulation. Eating and moderate activity within 2 hours. First scheduled wake after a long voyage feels disorienting — the colonist who boarded is the same person who exits, while everything they left behind has aged by decades.

title: Cryo-Sleep Technology
text:
Emergency Wake Protocol
Cryo pods monitor their own thermal environment continuously. If internal temperature exceeds the safe threshold — caused by external heat sources such as warp resonance drift, fire, power fault, or thermal damage from adjacent systems — the pod initiates emergency wake: rapid rewarming, wake drugs administered. The passenger wakes in 15–20 minutes, groggy but mobile.
Emergency wake bypasses the standard gradual rewarming. Recovery is harder: 1–2 hours of significant disorientation, nausea, temperature instability. Medically safe. Not comfortable.

title: Cryo-Sleep Technology
section: Emergency vs. Scheduled Wake: Recovery Profiles
text:
Emergency vs. Scheduled Wake: Recovery Profiles
The two protocols produce distinct recovery curves, which matters when multiple people wake under different circumstances in the same space.
Emergency wake fires a stress-response cocktail alongside the rewarming drugs. The body activates before the mind does — passengers are upright, mobile, and capable of basic action within 15–20 minutes. But higher cognition (calculation, judgment, pattern recognition) lags by 30–60 minutes. What feels like clarity is mostly adrenaline. There is a crash. Passengers who have been awake 2–3 hours after emergency wake are genuinely more functional than they were at minute fifteen.
Scheduled wake (crew-initiated, using crew pod protocol) is gradual rewarming without the stress cocktail. No immediate spike of stress-driven function. The passenger warms slowly and emerges properly — cognitive function and physical function arrive together, 30–60 minutes after the process begins. No crash. Slower to useful, but steadier once there.
The practical consequence: a crew member woken on scheduled protocol from a crew pod will appear less functional than an emergency-woken passenger in the first hour, even though their eventual recovery is better. In a crisis involving both, this creates a counterintuitive dynamic — the person everyone is waiting on is the most functional one in the room; they just haven’t arrived yet.

title: Cryo-Sleep Technology
text:
Resonance Sensitivity
Cryo pods are shielded against warp engine resonance up to a calibrated threshold. Above this threshold, the shielding itself heats fractionally. Sustained exposure above threshold triggers emergency wake — the pod reads heating as a threat and protects the passenger.
This is a safety feature. Sustained resonance exposure without wake would cause cellular damage; emergency wake is the lesser harm.
Under normal warp operation, engine resonance stays well below the threshold. The threshold can be exceeded by: engine calibration drift, coolant loss, drive damage, or abnormal mass distribution affecting resonance dampeners. The probability of this in any given voyage is low. The consequences when it occurs are significant.

title: Cryo-Sleep Technology
section: Single-Use Passenger Pods vs. Multi-Cycle Crew Pods
text:
Single-Use Passenger Pods vs. Multi-Cycle Crew Pods
Passenger pods (single-use): One cryo cycle certified. Safe for the initial freeze at departure and the scheduled wake at arrival. After emergency wake, re-cryo requires the full 48-hour pre-freeze protocol including fresh cellular protectant kits — not reusable, not carried in emergency quantities aboard CGSS vessels. Pods that have sustained thermal damage from a resonance event cannot be re-frozen regardless of consumable availability.
Crew pods (multi-cycle): Re-cryo capable. Precise thermal management, reusable prep cartridges, redundant monitoring across all cycle stages. Rated for the full number of crew rotation stints across a voyage’s lifespan. Cost approximately 40% more per unit than passenger-grade pods.
See generation-ships for the procurement economics behind this distinction.
The question “why can’t you just put them back to sleep?” surfaces naturally when passenger pods trigger emergency wake. The answer is technical, economic, and unambiguous: the capability was not specified, the consumables are not present, and the pods are damaged. There is no workaround.

title: Cryo-Sleep Technology
text:
Social Notes
A 30-year voyage, subjectively experienced, is a night’s sleep. Passengers board as one version of themselves and step off unchanged — except that the world they left is 30 years older or gone. Children they knew are middle-aged. Parents are dead. Languages have drifted. The colony they are joining has no cultural memory of Earth beyond what the Guides preserved.
Crew members experience the voyage differently. Rotating through multiple 3-month stints, they accumulate years of conscious experience during the voyage. A crew member completing a 30-year voyage has roughly 3–4 waking years behind them — and has watched waves of colonists sleep and wake while they aged, very slowly, in between. The social distance between crew and colonists upon arrival is not trivial.
Cryo is not considered dangerous in the Expansion Era. It is infrastructure. The psychological weight is not in the sleep — it is in the waking.

title: Chronology Protection
text:
Why the thorne-nexus is not a time machine, what has to go wrong for it to become one, and what the universe does about it when it does.
The thorne-nexus entry describes the gate network’s engineering and its politics. This is the layer underneath both: the reason the network has the shape it has, the reason it is laid the way it is laid, and the reason nobody is permitted to improve it.

title: Chronology Protection
text:
The problem
Faster-than-light signalling plus relativity equals travel into the past. This is not a matter of interpretation. If a signal can outrun light, and there exist observers in relative motion, then a signal that is instantaneous in one frame runs backwards in time in another. Chain two such signals through two different frames and the loop closes: the message arrives before it was sent.
The Nexus is FTL. Therefore the Nexus is, in principle, a time machine. Galactic civilization is built on top of an object that should not be allowed to exist.
It does exist, for three stacked reasons. Each of them is also a way it can fail.

title: Chronology Protection
text:
Barrier one — synchrony at construction
Both mouths of a gate pair are built together, in one place, in one frame, against one clock. They begin their existence with zero offset between them.
This is already the published constraint, arrived at for a different reason: signatures must match, so both ends must be constructed simultaneously in the same location. The signature requirement and the chronology requirement happen to demand the same thing. The engineers who discovered the first did not initially understand that they had also satisfied the second.

title: Chronology Protection
text:
Barrier two — dilation-free transport
A wormhole becomes a time machine by the Morris–Thorne–Yurtsever mechanism: take a pair of mouths with zero offset and move one of them relativistically. Differential aging accumulates between the mouths. Once the accumulated offset exceeds the light-travel time separating them through ordinary space, the pair is a time machine.
The recipe for building a time machine, in other words, is carry one end of a wormhole on a fast rocket.
The Nexus survives because of what carries its gates. Gate mouths are transported exclusively by Alcubierre vessels — and an Alcubierre ship accumulates no proper-time difference at all, because it never moves locally and never experiences dilation (see warp-drive). A gate carried thirty light-years by warp arrives with the same offset it left with: zero.
This is the real reason the galaxy lays gates with warp ships. Not economics, not tradition, not the deceleration advantage. A metric drive is the only transport method in existence that does not poison the cargo.

The transport law
The rule is usually stated absolutely — no gate mouth may be moved by a dilating method — but the underlying arithmetic is graded, and the grading is unexpectedly clean.
A mouth carried at velocity β arrives out of step with its twin by a fixed fraction of its own paradox threshold:

offset ÷ threshold = (1 − √(1 − β²)) ÷ β, which for modest speeds is very close to β ⁄ 2.

The remarkable part is what does not appear. Distance drops out. Duration drops out. A mouth carried one light-year and a mouth carried a thousand arrive with the same fraction of their margin spent, because the threshold scales with the distance exactly as fast as the accumulated dilation does. Only the speed matters.

This is why the prohibition sounds absolute in law and is not absolute in physics. Anything under roughly 0.2c is survivable. Anything above 0.8c is a weapon whether or not it was meant as one. And the Alcubierre drive is not merely the best option — it is the only one that spends nothing at all, which is a difference in kind rather than degree.
The corollary that reaches statute: no gate mouth may ever be moved by a dilating method. Forward sails, reaction drives, anything with a gamma. A sail-carried gate is not a cheaper gate. It is a weapon with a delivery date.
See propulsion for why sails are otherwise attractive, and why this rule costs the Empire real money every year.


The founding gates
The oldest mouths in the galaxy were carried by Orion pulse ships, at gamma, three hundred years at a time — which by the law above should have been catastrophic and was not.
Every Genesis seedship carried one half of a pre-paired set. The whole fleet was built in one place, at Sol, in the final decades before the Exodus, so pairing them was trivial and was done wholesale. Those pairs are the origin of the entire Nexus network; every later route hangs off them.
They arrived with about five percent of their margin already spent — one and a half years of offset against a thirty-year threshold, and less than that in practice, since a ship under acceleration and deceleration does not spend its whole voyage at cruise. Harmless individually. Permanent. Measurable, by anyone who thinks to measure.
Two consequences run from this through the whole of galactic history.
The founding network carries an inherited debt. Every original pair leans the same way, because every ship left the same star and braked at the far end. Those biases are small, they are real, and — the point — they sum along any path that strings them together. The Confederacy inherited a network whose safety margin was already five percent gone before anyone in it was born.
The founding topology is a tree, and it was chosen. The pairs were not assigned Sol-to-colony; Earth was not expected to survive, and did not. They were assigned colony-to-colony, in a pattern fixed before departure. That pattern contains no cycles. It was not an accident and it was not an emergent property of frontier economics: somebody sat down before the Exodus and drew a graph with no loops in it, knowing exactly why.
The Confederacy inherited the topology, inherited the doctrine of never closing a loop, and did not inherit the reason. For three thousand years the Great Houses enforced a rule whose justification had left with the people who wrote it.

title: Chronology Protection
text:
Barrier three — acyclic topology
The offsets of gates traversed in sequence add. A path that leaves a system through one gate, crosses to a third, and returns through a fourth accumulates the sum of every offset along the way.
A single gate with a small offset is harmless. A loop in the network that sums past threshold is a closed timelike curve spanning a thousand systems.
So the Nexus is maintained as a tree. No cycles. Ever. Every system hangs off exactly one route, and there is no alternate path to anywhere.
This is not how anyone would design a network. Redundancy is survivability, redundancy is cheaper logistics, redundancy is what every military planner and every trade guild in the Empire has petitioned for across three thousand years. They are refused every time, and the reason is not published.
Acyclic topology is containment. In a tree, a bad gate destroys itself and severs a branch: the damage is one gate and one region. In a cyclic network, a single poisoned mouth anywhere puts a closed timelike curve into a loop that may span half the galaxy — and the protection mechanism resolves the loop by destroying something in it, not necessarily the gate at fault.
The Empire accepts a catastrophically fragile network on purpose, to bound the blast radius of a failure it cannot otherwise survive. It is the largest firebreak ever built, and almost nobody knows it is a firebreak.

title: Chronology Protection
text:
What natural drift does — nothing
Worth stating explicitly, because it is the assumption everything else rests on.
The two mouths of a gate sit in different gravitational potentials and move at different orbital velocities, so they do accumulate offset just by existing. The rate is of order one part in a billion. Across the entire Imperial Era that comes to roughly a minute and a half, against a threshold measured in decades.
Natural drift is seven orders of magnitude short and always will be. Gates do not age into time machines. This is precisely why the network is trusted, why gate certification focuses on provenance rather than on scheduled retirement — and why the poisoning attack works so well. Everyone knows gates are safe. Everyone is right, until someone lies about where a gate has been.

title: Chronology Protection
section: When protection fails — the Hawking mechanism
text:
When protection fails — the Hawking mechanism
Hawking’s chronology protection conjecture is not a decree that paradoxes are forbidden. It proposes a mechanism: as a closed timelike curve approaches formation, vacuum fluctuations circulate through the incipient loop and reinforce themselves without bound. The stress-energy diverges at the Cauchy horizon. The apparatus is destroyed before the curve can close.
The universe does not prevent the paradox. It destroys whatever was about to cause it.
In practice, a gate approaching threshold does not fail quietly or gracefully. The throat begins to radiate — first as a rising acoustic and electromagnetic signature that gate crews describe, invariably and independently, as a hum. The divergence is exponential. From the first detectable signature to the destruction of the gate and everything sharing its station is a matter of days.
Nexus crews are trained on the hum. There is no procedure for stopping it. The procedure is evacuation.

title: Chronology Protection
text:
The poisoned gate
The attack follows from the barriers. Build a gate pair legitimately. Transport one mouth on a Forward sail instead of a warp vessel. Deliver it, certified, into a rival’s network.
The arithmetic: a sail running at 0.9c crosses thirty light-years in about thirty-three years of coordinate time and roughly fourteen of its own. The delivered mouth arrives some nineteen years out of step with its twin, against a threshold of thirty.
Nineteen against thirty. The gate works. It opens, it carries traffic, it passes every functional test, and it will do so indefinitely. It is loaded and it is not fired.
What fires it is a loop. Splice that gate into a network path that closes a cycle — or add a second compromised mouth anywhere along the same circuit — and the offsets sum past threshold. The hum starts somewhere in the loop, and not necessarily where the crime was committed.
This is why gate provenance is the most sensitive category of information the Great Houses hold. Not expiry dates: transport records. A House’s real vulnerability is the gates it cannot certify — gates acquired in war, gates whose construction archives burned, gates inherited from Houses that no longer exist. Every major House is running at least one gate whose history it cannot fully account for, and using it daily, and hoping.
Demanding a provenance audit of a rival’s gate is, correctly understood, an accusation of mass murder. It is never a routine request.

title: Chronology Protection
text:
The Runners
A superluminal warp bubble is a causality violation by construction. Why does the universe tolerate the Runners?
Because they are sealed. Nothing enters a superluminal bubble and nothing leaves it. A Runner cannot signal, cannot be signalled, cannot be boarded, cannot be intercepted by anything that would not immediately become a second Runner. It cannot participate in a loop.
It is a causality violation that cannot be used, and protection only bites where a curve would actually close.
Which reframes the seal entirely. The horizon that traps a Runner’s crew is not an unfortunate side effect of the geometry. It is the protection, arriving early and doing its work quietly. The universe does not stop a ship from crossing c. It stops the ship from telling anyone.
The two exotic technologies of this civilization fail in the same way, for the same reason. One is sealed so it cannot speak; the other detonates when it would. Both are the same law, applied at different volumes.

title: Chronology Protection
text:
The Great Scattering
The published record says communications were lost, that the Empire’s networks depended on synthetic technology, that knowledge was lost and populations scattered. All of that stands. Underneath it is a mechanism.
The Nexus did not decay. It went off.
Three thousand years of firebreak doctrine held because the tree held. The Synthetic Wars broke the tree — gates laid without certification under wartime conditions, routes spliced in desperation to restore contact with cut-off regions, provenance archives destroyed along with the institutions that kept them. Cycles appeared in a network that had never been permitted one.
Then one compromised mouth, somewhere, in some loop, summed past threshold.
The cascade is what a firebreak doctrine looks like when it collapses: not a slow decline in service but a sequence of stations annihilating themselves across the galaxy over a span of years, each loss re-routing traffic into loops that had not existed the day before. Every gate that survived became more dangerous as its neighbours died.
The Scattering is self-inflicted physics. The synths did not do it. Nobody did it. It was the accumulated consequence of three thousand years of a rule that everyone obeyed and almost nobody understood, broken once under pressure by people acting in good faith.
And because a tree that loses edges does not degrade but shatters, what remained was not a thinner network. It was thousands of disconnected fragments that could no longer reach each other by any means — which is the Great Scattering, and which is why it is called that.
The survivors did not know why. They still do not. History records that the gates began to sing.
See also: thorne-nexus, warp-drive, propulsion, galactic-timeline.
