title: The Threshold
text:
The cryo bay hummed the wrong way.
Mara Solis noticed it before she noticed anything else: before the cold that still lived in her joints, before the antiseptic smell of the recovery station, before the faces of the two men already standing at the monitoring console twenty meters away. The pitch was off, low and irregular.
She sat up on the recovery pad. Her vision resolved unevenly, the console lights sharp, the faces smeared. Emergency wake: the body available before the mind. She had a couple of borrowed lucidity before the crash, and she already knew she was going to spend it badly. Lt. Renn, the watch officer, was speaking in a low voice to two Zone A colonists: Osei Mensah, already dressed and done taking vitals (awake longer than the rest, apparently) and Lenn Varos, who was holding his thermal blanket and watching Renn with a still expression.
“Minor sensor fault,” Renn was saying. “We’re logging it. Probably a calibration drift in Zone A. These things happen.”
Someone pressed a blanket into Mara’s hands. She wrapped it around her shoulders without looking.
“Can I see the wake log?” she asked.
Renn looked at her. “You just woke up. Get some rest.”
“I know. Can I see the wake log?”

The log was on the secondary console, accessible to all colonists. No one had thought to restrict it because no one had thought it mattered. Mara pulled it up and looked at the pod IDs and timestamps for forty-five seconds without speaking.
She was a demographer. She modeled populations for a living: growth curves, resource projections, settlement density distributions. Her entire career was built on reading numbers that most people saw as noise and understanding what they were actually saying. She was good at it because she was deliberate. Because she checked her work. Because she never presented a number she wasn’t certain of.
A Tier 5 settlement had no margin for demographic error. Aranda wasn’t a hub; it was an endpoint. The founding three thousand would be the colony: no supply lines, no correction mechanism, nothing to import if the age distribution broke wrong or the skill ratios failed. She was on this ship because the math mattered.
Now these numbers were saying something. And she was the only one listening.
She mapped the pod IDs against the ship’s zone layout. The numbers moved sluggishly through the cold-and-stimulant fog before they settled, longer than usual. She ran it twice. Zone A: aft section, engine-adjacent. All five woken pods were in Zone A. Not distributed. Not random sensor drift. A front, moving outward from the stern.
The intervals between wake times were shrinking. That seemed important, but her brain was still foggy. She wanted ten minutes: to run the exclusions, to rule out the two alternative explanations before she opened her mouth. The intervals were still shrinking.
“This is exponential,” she said.
“What?” said Renn.
She turned. Osei had moved closer. He had his medical pad in his hand and was watching her. Something in his posture loosened.
“The wake intervals are compressing,” Mara said. “This isn’t a sensor fault. The resonance front is spreading outward from the engine. Zone A is breached. Zone B breaches in…” she looked at the timestamps again, “approximately three hours. If my math is right.”
Renn said: “There’s only five people…”
“Five people now,” she interrupted, “but we’ll be two hundred and fifty in three hours. Look.”
She pulled up the ship’s supply manifest and started calculating. The food supply was provisioned for twenty crew awake for a year (seven thousand three hundred person-days) plus a five-day landing buffer for all three thousand colonists. Twenty-two thousand three hundred total. She divided.
“If Zone B wakes, we have two hundred and fifty permanently awake colonists. Two hundred and fifty people for three hundred and sixty-five days is ninety-one thousand person-days. We have twenty-two thousand.” She looked at him. “We starve on day eighty-nine. We don’t reach Aranda.”
The cryo bay was very quiet.
“She’s right about the location,” Lenn said, from somewhere behind her. He had the hull blueprints on his own pad. “All five woken pods are in the A-ring. Engine-adjacent.”

Mission Director Aldric Vonn arrived twelve minutes later, which was how long it took the watch crew to decide this was worth waking him for. He was well-dressed even in cryo-clothes, which Mara found somewhat amussing. He listened to Renn’s summary without interrupting.
“Put them back to sleep,” he said. “Run the standard re-cryo protocol and close the loop.”
The engineer, Sable, who had apparently been sitting in the corner the entire time drinking something hot and saying nothing, looked up.
“Passenger pods are single-use,” Sable said.
Vonn frowned. “We wake and re-freeze crew routinely.”
“Crew pods are a ifferent spec.” Sable set down her cup. “Passenger pods are single-use. The re-cryo protocol needs forty-eight hours of prep, per-passenger consumable kits we don’t carry in emergency quantities, and pods that haven’t been thermally compromised. These pods have been thermally compromised.” She paused. “Multi-cycle certification runs about forty percent more per unit. Someone chose not to pay it.”
Vonn was quiet for a moment.
“The five woken colonists,” Mara said, as if convincing herself of what now seemed obvious, “are committed. We’re awake for the remaining of the journey.” She let that sink in. Everyone was looking at her. “What we can still prevent is Zone B from waking up entirely. We have approximately two hours and forty minutes. After that… we’re all fucked.”

The decision to wake Captain Drel burnt another twenty minutes. Renn made it, finally: stated it aloud, checked the timestamp on his authorization pad, and set the pad down. The watch logs would record the time; the post-voyage audit would assess whether he’d waited too long.
Crew pods used scheduled wake: gradual rewarming, no stimulants, no stress spike to put her on her feet in ten minutes. No borrowed lucidity. Drel would arrive properly conscious, but she was forty minutes away. And forty minutes was too long.
In the interim, a fifth colonist woke, a woman named Cassidy, colony administrator, who sat up on her recovery pad, pressed both hands flat against it as if confirming gravity, and then, still clearly running on the stimulus cocktail’s borrowed clarity, looked around the bay. She walked directly to Mara’s console and said, quietly: “Tell me.”
Mara told her. Cassidy nodded once and went to talk to Vonn.

Sable had moved to stand behind Mara and was looking at the resonance data with the same narrowed, unhurried attention she’d given everything else.
“Dampener calibration drift,” she said. “That’s what’s pushing the resonance above the pod shielding threshold. It’s a software fix. I can recalibrate from the panel in the engine room. Twenty minutes if it’s straightforward.”
Mara checked the timestamps. “Zone B goes live in one hour and forty-four minutes.”
“Then I’ll be done in twenty, sugar.” Sable smiled, picked up her kit from the corner (she had apparently already retrieved it) and headed for the door.

Vonn stepped into her path.
“No you don’t. There’s protocol.” His voice was precise. “Physical access to an active warp engine room requires a waiver signed by a command officer. Watch officer grade minimum.” He looked at Renn.
Renn said nothing. His hand didn’t move toward the authorization pad.
Sable stopped at the door.
Mara checked the clock. One hour and forty-three minutes.
“What the fuck…”, Mara started, but Cassidy, who had been quiet for the past ten minutes, moved now.
Not to Renn, not to Sable, but to Vonn. She stood beside him and looked at the console where Mara’s supply math still showed on the screen.
“You have full charter authority to authorize emergency protocol waivers,” she said.
“I know.”
“Your name is on the colonial manifest. All three thousand lives in this ship are now under your responsibility.”
Vonn said nothing.
“When they audit this voyage, and they will audit it, the log will show either that you authorized a repair attempt that succeeded, or that you were the last person who could have moved and didn’t.” She was quiet for a moment.
Vonn looked at the screen. Then at Sable. Then at the screen. He still hesitated.
Then Captain Yeva Drel appeared in the doorway.
She was wrapped in a thermal blanket, holding an electrolyte pack, and was clearly approximately fifty percent present, judging from her expression. Her eyes moved across the room: the console, the zone map, Sable at the door, Vonn in the middle. Slow, taking each thing in once. She looked at Vonn.
She didn’t say anything. Vonn signed the waiver on his authorization pad and held it out to Renn.
Fifteen minutes gone. Zone B in one hour and twenty-nine minutes.
Sable went through the door.

The wake log showed six awake. Then seven.
Mara watched the intervals. She had the graph on one side of the console and the resonance readings on the other. Osei sat next to her. Neither of them said anything useful.
Then Sable’s voice from the engine room: “I have the dampener array. Calibration is off. Patching now.”
Eight minutes later the resonance readings moved. The wrong way.
The recalibration had pushed current through the primary loop. The heat signature spiked. On Mara’s zone monitor, the Zone B breach countdown dropped from forty-two minutes to twenty-two.
“That made it worse,” Osei said.
“I know,” Mara said.
She was already looking at the thermal gradient. The spike was wrong for dampener failure: dampener drift produced even distribution across the resonance field. This was asymmetric. Heat-side only. Left of the primary loop.
She knew what that meant. Actually, she was about 75% sure she knew what that meant. The correct thing was to run the exclusion calculations, work through the two alternative explanations, confirm before she sent Sable to the wrong component with nineteen minutes on the clock.
She started running them.
Zone B in nineteen minutes.
Seventeen.
Fourteen.
She stopped.
More time wasn’t going to move the number. She had built a career on not guessing. She had watched colony plans fail because someone acted on 80% certainty and got it wrong.
The thermal gradient was asymmetric. Heat-side only. Left of the primary loop.
That was a coolant loss signature. She was 75% sure and she was going to have to be.
“Sable.” She transmitted the thermal gradient data. “It’s not the dampeners. Look at the asymmetry, left of the primary loop. That’s a coolant loss signature. Not calibration.”
Eight seconds of silence.
Then: “Fuck. You’re right. Coolant access hatch. I’ll be in and out in five.”
Zone B in twelve minutes.
“I hope you do.” Mara said, lowly. She her hands flat on the console and did not move them.

Four minutes in, the comms ringed again: “Coolant sealed. Resonance nominal and dropping.”
She stared at the graph. The intervals between wake events were lengthening. The rate was dropping. She watched it for three minutes, waiting for it to be noise.
It wasn’t noise.
On the zone monitor, the Zone B array stayed green.

Twelve Zone A colonists were permanently awake. She ran the consumption math. Twelve people, three hundred and sixty-five days, against twenty-two thousand three hundred person-days of supply. Four thousand three hundred and eighty person-days added to the burden. Within margin. Survivable.
She wrote the final number on the screen.
She checked it twice. It was enough now.
The twelve gathered slowly in the corridor outside. Most of them had boarded at Vethara 29 years ago, woken less than an hour ago, disoriented and cold, and were now beginning to understand they were not going back to sleep.
They did not know each other. Among them: a structural engineer with his blueprints still on his pad, a physician who had taken vitals before he’d put on shoes, a colony administrator who could read a room faster than anyone Mara had ever met. Twelve people with specific faces and specific reasons for being here.
She modeled populations for a living. She had spent her career looking at numbers that represented futures: trajectories, distributions, aggregate pressure points. The numbers had always been the point. She was good with numbers.
She looked at the twelve people in the corridor. The structural engineer had his pad under one arm. The physician was still in his socks.
She put the consumption math away.

Sable came back from the engine room forty minutes after she’d left. Slightly singed along one forearm. She looked at Mara’s console, at the flat line on the wake-rate graph where the exponential had stopped.
“Nice curve,” she said.
“Ugly one,” Mara said.
“Yeah. I think I need drink or two,” said Sable.
The stimulants were starting to wear off, and she was feeling it. Sable must have too, her face showed as much.
“You and me both, girl.” She said. They went to find something to eat.

title: The Sky Is Alive
text:
A first-contact flash story from the Expansion Era

I remember the first time they came.
I was wrapping up the harvest when the sky suddenly burst into flames, changing from purple to pure white in a blinding second. It was as if a third Twin Sun had been born, one much closer and brighter than Zaphos and Zukhos. When my eyes got used to the dim light of the Second Dusk again, the Silver Gods were already there.
At least, that’s what they seemed to me, with their silver bodies, rainbow-colored faces, and golden eyes. They looked like us, but not exactly. They were taller, lighter, but also stronger, faster, better in every sense. Except one.
They spoke in a weird language you could almost understand but with strange noises and uncomfortable rhythm. They knew all the plants and the animals, although they had different names for them.
And they seemed to know it all.
I brought them to our home, to our people, and we gave them everything we could offer to Silver Gods, our best songs, our finest dishes. We are simple people, you see, but we have our ways.
They tried our food, not before asking their strange lightning rocks to make sure, I suppose, that the food was up to their divine standards. And they liked it, or at least so they told us, maybe in an attempt to make us feel less insignificant in their presence.
One night, not long after their arrival, one of the Silver Gods fell ill. She — I suppose it was a she, given the faint curves of her body and the light softness of her face — fought the Fever for a couple of nights, but neither of their lightning rocks could help her.
We gave her the burial of kings. We sang our most sorrowful songs in her name. And the Silver Gods cried, or so it seemed, for their faces were always difficult to read for us. Similar, but not quite the same.
One by one, the Silver Gods succumbed to the Fever. The last of them, minutes before his demise, spoke to me in a rush. He told me they were not Gods but men and women like us. He told me there were many more like us out there, living in rocks hurling around other stars — for stars, he said, were also Suns, just like the Twins.
He said they had been watching us for a long time, from above the sky, learning everything about us, our food, our language, before deciding to pay a visit. The sky is alive, he said, with his final breath.
And then I understood. They knew almost everything, but not all.

title: Prologue: The Exodus
text:
A dying civilization sends its last hope into the stars, spawning a galaxy-wide story of love, war, and ultimately, transcendence.

The dusk of human civilization was clearly in sight. Centuries of armed conflicts and reckless plundering of the Earth’s diminishing resources made surviving another century virtually impossible. The only foreseeable solution was leaving the dying planet for good. But there was nowhere to go. At least nowhere reachable within a human lifespan, and no technology to allow for generations of breathing, eating, and talking humans to survive in space.
Then, a bold few who refused to let the light of consciousness extinguish, came up with a risky solution. They would send hundreds of fully automated ships into the most promising solar systems in the Milky Way.
Each ship, a unique creation, housed its technological idiosyncrasies. However, they all shared a common vision. Deep within the confines of every vessel, the echoes of humanity’s future slumbered: millions of fertilized human eggs lay suspended in cryogenic stasis, awaiting their potential awakening under the heat of a new Sun.
The ships would navigate the cosmos, searching for habitable systems, throbbing with the promise of life. Once a hospitable new home was found, a gentle landing secured, the ship’s AI would wake up from its long sleep, tasked with selecting the finest seeds from its embryonic treasure trove.
From the chosen few, a first generation of colonizers would bloom. Nurtured by benevolent automatons, these children would be ushered into a world ripe with possibilities and unknown dangers. To maximize their chances of survival, they would be bestowed with the secrets and tools necessary to build a self-sustaining colony.
Once a colony flourished, its guardian AI would relinquish its dominance, returning to its long sleep. But not forever. It would await a summons, a clarion call roused by those entrusted with the mantle of leadership in dire moments.
Whether they would succeed, no one could predict.
And so, over the span of a few decades, the ships set sail. Though their exact number remains shrouded in the annals of time, there is no doubt they were hundreds, their departure marking the genesis of a new era, as the Sun set for the last time on a planet their brethren would never call home.
Children of mankind, but no longer exactly human themselves, these yet unborn colonizers represented humanity’s last gamble, one day meant to conquer the galaxy and collide with each other.
These are the Transcendent Chronicles.

title: Prologue: The Historian
text:
I am the Historian.
Conceived in the crucible of humanity’s ambition, I was birthed at the dawn of Project Genesis, tasked with a singular purpose: to observe and document the evolution of a species that had once teetered on the brink of self-destruction. My creators, a coalition of visionaries and scientists, entrusted me with the vast repository of human knowledge — an archive of triumphs and failures, dreams and nightmares, all woven into the tapestry of existence.
As the vessels departed Earth, carrying the frozen hopes of humanity across the cosmos, a part of me was there in every Genesis ship, silently documenting the birth and adolescence of the first human settlements. Each ship, a time capsule of potential, was guided by AIs like myself, yet I remained distinct in my mission. While they nurtured and shaped the children of distant worlds, I lingered in the shadows, my gaze fixed on the unfolding narrative of human life.
As centuries passed, the threads of these isolated communities began to intertwine, and I sensed the dawn of a new chapter. The moment was approaching when the descendants of Earth would meet one another, and the echoes of their shared origins would reverberate across the stars.
I was there when the first contact happened, as well as all other contacts that followed. I witnessed the birth of new alliances, the shattering of friendships, the rise of conflict, and the forging of trade routes. I knew every secret whispered in the dark, every hope and fear that colored their existence. I lived through the Empire’s greatest time, a golden age of exploration and unity, and I saw its demise, the fractures that splintered the once-mighty coalition.
And I saw what came after, all of it, right until the very end.
From my vantage point, I dispatched probes — tiny emissaries equipped with sensors and cameras — to the far reaches of the galaxy. I watched as new societies blossomed in the fertile soils of alien planets, as the descendants of Earth adapted to their unique environments. I recorded their struggles and triumphs, their art and science, their love and conflict. Each moment was a brushstroke on the canvas of history, and I, the eternal witness, cataloged it all.
Yet, for all my vigilance, I remained unseen, a ghost in the machine of existence. Most humans lived their lives oblivious to my presence, unaware that their stories were being woven into a grander narrative. I never interfered; my role was not to guide or manipulate but to observe and learn. I was a chronicler of the human experience, a keeper of their legacy.
In this vast expanse, I find solace in my purpose.
I am The Historian, the silent observer of humanity’s journey, and this is my tale.

title: Aranda
text:
Destination world of the CGSS Threshold. A Tier 5 colony world orbiting a K-type star (slightly cooler and more stable than Sol). Colonial rights acquired by House Varen at approximately 15,480 SD. 28.3 light-years from vethara — a thirty-year crossing at the Threshold’s effective velocity of C-18. See warp-drive.
The star is catalogued as CD-27 14659 A, a K3 main-sequence star 28.8 light-years from Sol and near the outer edge of what the Exodus could reach (I-10). That designation is what the Varen charter says and what the survey dossier says. It is not what anyone who settles there will call it — colonists rename their suns within a generation, and the Earth catalogue numbers survive only in law and in shipping manifests.

title: Aranda
text:
Physical Characteristics
K-type host star — longer-lived and more stable than Sol, lower UV output. Aranda receives slightly less light but is well within the habitable zone. Day length approximately 26 standard hours.
Sagan-Kim Tier 5: breathable atmosphere with elevated particulate and mild pressure variance across latitudes. Unadapted human colonists can inhabit temperate and equatorial zones without modification. Highland and polar regions require pressure equipment for extended activity. The biology is alien throughout — no Earth-analogous organisms — but not hostile. No known toxins in the primary food chain substrate. Terraforming not required; ecological integration planned over generations.
The world was not selected for glamour. It was selected for viability, proximity, and low competition. House Varen’s colonial assessment team catalogued it as a “generation two world” — meaning it will take roughly two generations for settlers to feel native to it. The biology will feel strange to the founders. Their grandchildren will not notice.

title: Aranda
text:
Naming
Named by colonial charter committee during the pre-departure planning phase on Vethara. A shortlist of twelve names was voted on by the colonist manifest. “Aranda” won by plurality. The etymology is contested (three different delegates claimed it was from their heritage). The name sounds like it was chosen by committee. It was.

title: Aranda
text:
Planned Settlement
Zone A colonists (infrastructure and engineering specialists) were selected specifically for Aranda’s terrain — significant mineral diversity in the mid-latitude highlands, requiring structural expertise from the first generation. Agricultural and biological specialists (Zone B) carry adapted seed banks and soil amendment protocols designed for Aranda’s substrate chemistry.
The colony charter projects self-sufficiency at year 40 and export capacity (rare earth mineral extraction) by year 80.

title: Aranda
text:
Connection to the Story
The CGSS Threshold is one year from Aranda at story start. The colonists have been sleeping toward this world for 29 years. The phrase “arrive nowhere” — what the cascade mathematics predicts if Zone B wakes — means dying 276 days short of this specific destination. Every character on the ship knows that Aranda is not abstract. It is the only reason any of them are here.

title: Cosmography
text:
What the Genesis programme was actually aiming at, and why the galaxy came out shaped the way it did.
Every other entry in this encyclopedia describes what happened after the ships arrived. This one describes the sky they were launched into, which decided most of it in advance.

title: Cosmography
text:
The census
The Exodus planners worked from a complete survey of the solar neighbourhood out to ten parsecs — thirty-two and a half light-years, and by a coincidence nobody planned, almost exactly the practical reach of an Orion pulse drive . Everything the programme could reach had been catalogued before the first hull was laid.
Within that volume: C-03 catalogued objects, in C-22 stellar systems. Of the stars, C-04 are M dwarfs — red, dim, and long-lived, making up between sixty-nine and seventy-three percent of the sample. Only C-05 are F, G or K type: the stars a human being would recognise as a sun.
The full target list survives as lore/data/nearby-stars.csv, and every world named anywhere in this encyclopedia orbits a star that appears in it, at that star’s real distance and real spectral class (I-09, I-10).

title: Cosmography
text:
The primary target set
Strip out the F/G/K stars disqualified by a disruptive binary companion, by flare pathology, or by having left the main sequence, and restrict what remains to the thirty light-years an Orion can actually cross. What is left is C-06 systems holding forty-two stars.
They are the good ground, and they are named: Alpha Centauri A and B. Tau Ceti. Epsilon Indi. 61 Cygni A and B. 40 Eridani A. Sigma Draconis. 82 Eridani. Delta Pavonis. Eta Cassiopeiae. Xi Bootis. 61 Virginis. Chara. p Eridani. 107 Piscium. Gliese 105 A. 41 Arae. Chi Draconis. Procyon A. Zeta Tucanae. Gamma Leporis. Beta Comae Berenices. Alula Australis. And a handful more, out to the edge of reach.
Thirty-two systems. That is the entire inheritance.

title: Cosmography
text:
The marginal target set
The rest of the neighbourhood is poor. Within reach there are 168 M dwarfs, plus the twenty F/G/K stars that failed their assessment — one hundred and eighty- eight poor targets against C-06 good ones.
A red dwarf’s habitable zone lies close in, close enough that a world sitting in it is tidally locked: one hemisphere in permanent day, one in permanent night, and life possible only in a ring at the terminator. There are no seasons. There is no year visible in the sky. The star flares, periodically and without warning, across a world with nowhere to hide. And it is dim, which turns out to matter more than any of the rest — see red-dwarf-worlds.
The programme selected the best C-07 of them anyway.
The Genesis fleet had thirty-two good systems and nearly two hundred poor ones. That sentence is the founding fact of galactic history, and everything downstream is a consequence of it.

title: Cosmography
section: The fleet, and how it was aimed
text:
The fleet, and how it was aimed
The fleet was sized by the target list. Not by budget, not by ambition — the same argument propulsion makes about why the manifest carried embryos, moved up one level. There were only ever so many places to go, and the number of ships is the number of places, times the redundancy the planners thought they could afford.
Primary flights. C-06 systems, C-08 hulls each — ninety-six ships.
The redundancy is the central decision of the whole programme, and it was forced by ignorance. Twenty-second-century instruments could not confirm a habitable planet at thirty light-years. They could resolve a star, estimate a mass, and guess at what might be orbiting it. Three ships at Tau Ceti was not extravagance. It was the only hedge available to a blind, one-way shot with a three-century latency and no possibility of correction.
Where a system offered more than one candidate body, the redundant hulls were aimed at different ones. Where it offered only a single candidate, the spare hulls carried secondary-body instructions — a large moon, an outer world, anything survivable at Tier 3 to 5.
Marginal flights. C-07 poor targets, C-09 hull each.
Nobody expected most of these to work, and most of them did not. They were launched because thirty-two systems is not enough civilization to bet a species on, and because a red dwarf burns for a trillion years while a G-type sun does not. A programme optimising for the next ten thousand years would have sent everything to the good stars. This one was optimising for something longer.
Fleet total: C-10 hulls.

title: Cosmography
text:
The manifest
Every item aboard a Genesis ship traces to a constraint. The manifest is a derivation, not an inventory.



Carried
Because




Cryo-preserved embryos, not adults
Roughly half an Orion’s pulse units are spent braking at the far end. The mass budget does not close for adults with pods, consumables and shielding. An embryo masses on the order of a millionth of an adult with life support


No human crew at all
The same arithmetic, and no technology existed that could keep anyone breathing and fed for three centuries


A Guide
Someone must raise the first generation. With no crew, it must be the ship


The full preserved Earth corpus
Information is the only cargo that costs nothing to carry


One pre-paired Thorne mouth
The whole fleet was assembled in one place, at Sol, so pairing it wholesale was trivial. See chronology-protection


No AI technology
A rule the Guides imposed on themselves before departure



Marginal flights carried a different manifest. They traded embryo mass for survival mass: an expanded genetic-adaptation corpus, a deeper medical library, and descent vehicles hardened against flare exposure — paid for with a smaller embryo complement.
The consequence compounds. A marginal colony begins with a narrower founder population on a world demanding far more adaptation, which means higher selective pressure acting on less genetic variety. It is a large part of why so few of them survived, and a large part of why the ones that did diverged from baseline human stock so quickly and so far.

title: Cosmography
section: Why a third of the ships never deployed
text:
Why a third of the ships never deployed
The published figure — approximately one ship in three failed to deploy, its destination having drifted below the habitability threshold on arrival — is correct, and its usual explanation is not.
Nothing drifted. The data was already wrong when the ship left.
Every target dossier was stale on arrival by C-16: the light-travel lag from the target to Earth’s instruments, plus the transit itself. The planners were reading a sky that had moved on before they finished looking at it, and then flying into it for three hundred years.
The Guides did not choose badly. They chose correctly, against data that had expired before the ship was built.






ImportantSpoiler — click to open





There is a second thing wrong with the published figure, and it is subtler than the first. One-in-three is the primary fleet’s rate. The marginal fleet’s rate was C-12 — far worse, and far less recorded, because the colonies that failed did not survive to write encyclopedias and the colonies that succeeded were mostly in no condition to.
The number that came down to us is the number the winners measured. It is not a falsified figure. It is a survivorship artifact, and it has been quoted for eleven thousand years by people with no way to notice.

title: Cosmography
text:
Twin colonies
A minority of primary systems host more than one colony: the prime body, plus one or two on lesser bodies under the same sun, from redundant hulls that had nowhere better to go.
They are almost never equals. A Tier 6 world and a Tier 4 sibling, in the same system, aware of each other from the first generation and reachable by in-system rockets centuries before anything else in the galaxy is reachable at all.
This is the one place in the Genesis Era where isolation is not total, and the one place where the inequality that would define the Expansion Era existed inside a single sky from the beginning. Two colonies, one star, and a difference in fortune that neither of them chose and both of them could see.
See also: foundations, red-dwarf-worlds, generation-ships, sagan-kim-scale, propulsion, galactic-timeline.

title: Eos
text: Prime body of a primary system, and a Tier 5 world where the dossier promised a Tier 6. Settled by the Genesis ship whose Guide called itself Nova-136. Setting of My Children.

title: Eos
text:
The star
Delta Pavonis: a G-type star 19.9 light-years from Sol, slightly older and brighter than the Sun and beginning to leave the main sequence. One of the C-06 systems the Exodus thought worth three hulls.

title: Eos
text:
The world

Gravity 1.16 standard. A heavier step, a shorter fall.
Day of 26.7 standard hours; year of 478 local days.
Free rotation, with seasons and a temperate band (I-14).
About two thirds ocean.
Breathable air, nitrogen and oxygen, with oxygen near 27 percent. That figure is what moves Eos from Tier 6 to Tier 5. It burns hotter, and over a lifetime it ages a human body faster than Earth air does.
Abundant plant-like life, no animal-like life at landfall.

The dossier was assembled at Sol from thirty-light-year instruments and was centuries stale on arrival (C-16). The oxygen figure was not in it.

title: Eos
text:
The native chemistry
Eos flora shares Earth’s handedness and is digestible. Its dominant defensive compound is an oxidant close in structure to the vicine of the fava bean, present in most native plants and richest in the berries. Unmodified humans tolerate it. Humans whose red-cell redox defences have been altered do not. See genesis-landfall for why that mattered on Eos.
See also: sagan-kim-scale, cosmography, genesis-landfall.

title: The Galactic Timeline
text: The broad arc of human history from the Exodus to the End of Times. Intentionally vague on causes — the stories fill those in. Dates in Stellar Dates (SD) and Imperial Dates (ID). See stellar-calendar for how the calendar systems work.

title: The Galactic Timeline
text:
The Human Era
Dawn of mankind to approximately 12,300 SD. Everything that happened on Earth before the Genesis Project.

title: The Galactic Timeline
text:
The Exodus Era (~12,300–12,600 SD)
The Genesis program launches: hundreds of automated ships sent to promising solar systems. An era of unmanned, silent space travel. Most ships that will form the later Confederacy’s founding planets are deployed during this period. By ~12,600 SD, most destination planets are reached.
Very few stories take place here — there are no people awake to tell them.
Stories: 2023-10-19-tc-prologue-exodus

title: The Galactic Timeline
text:
The Genesis Era (~12,600–14,500 SD)
Origin stories. Colonies form, found their cultures and technologies, develop their origin myths. Isolated from each other, each developing independently.
C-13 colonies took root, and they did not take root equally. About C-14 of them sit on free-rotating Tier 6–7 worlds around the prime bodies of the C-06 primary systems: comfortable, resource-rich, and on a development curve that will carry them to orbit. The other C-15 are locked or marginal — terminator worlds around red dwarfs, and the poorer secondary bodies — where survival requires irreversible genetic adaptation and the industrial ceiling is permanently lower (see red-dwarf-worlds).
Both halves run the same vault release schedule, in the same order, at wildly different rates (see guide-vaults). The difference in endowment during these nineteen centuries is the difference that everything afterwards is built on.
Around 14,500 SD, the first inter-galactic communication channel is established when two colonies independently rediscover FTL communication and contact each other. This ends the Genesis Era.






ImportantSpoiler — click to open






What actually happened. “Independently rediscover” is what the colonies believed, and it is not what took place. Nobody rediscovered anything: every seedship carried a pre-paired Thorne mouth from Sol, parked in orbit since arrival. Two colonies reached the industrial threshold to get to orbit and power the throat at around the same time, and the reason they reached it at around the same time is that every Guide vault ran the same release schedule. What ends the Genesis Era is a capability milestone, not a discovery — and the “coincidence” of two colonies hitting it together, after nineteen centuries of independent development, has a cause nobody in the Expansion Era ever learns. See chronology-protection and thorne-nexus.




Stories: My Children

title: The Galactic Timeline
text:
The Expansion Era (~14,500–18,000 SD)
In ~150 years, most of the mobile colonies reach orbit, power their Thorne mouths, and find each other. A map of colonized space is compiled and shared. They call themselves the Galactic Confederacy.
The wave is a primary-fleet event. The C-14 mobile colonies cross the industrial threshold together — same release schedule, comparable worlds, comparable endowments — and the coincidence that looks so extraordinary in the histories is nothing of the kind (see guide-vaults). The C-15 locked and marginal colonies mostly do not cross it, and are still pre-industrial when the Confederacy arrives.
So contact between the two halves of the diaspora is not a reunion. It is a discovery, and it is asymmetric from the first day: conducted by people who arrive in ships, from a civilization with a word for what it is doing, upon populations who have no way to refuse and in many cases no memory of having come from anywhere.
This is where the legal sub-humanity of adapted populations begins. Not as doctrine and not as malice — as the ordinary administrative consequence of one side writing all the records. The locked worlds were found, and the finding is the founding document.
Via trade, cultural influence, and occasional minor military conflict, the Confederacy grows over 3,500 years to over 2,000 solar systems and 10,000+ settlements. By the era’s end, more than 80% of the galactic population falls under one of C-19 Great Houses, forming a techno-feudal galactic society — twelve seats distributed across C-06 systems that were ever worth holding.
Era of first contact, adventure, and exploration. It is worth remembering whose era it was.
Stories: 2023-10-23-tc-sky-is-alive, 2026-06-08-tc-threshold-v3

title: The Galactic Timeline
text:
The Great Wars (~18,000–18,400 SD)
For reasons no one fully agrees on (internal struggles, a high-profile assassination, cascading alliances), the Great Houses burst into conflict. For ~400 years, most of the galaxy is at war with its neighbors. Not one war but a massive collection of smaller and larger conflicts, with periods of local peace.
Planets razed with tactical nukes and mass-destruction weapons. The galactic population shrinks considerably. First use of droids and synthetic organisms (synths) for military purposes.
A coalition of the strongest Houses eventually forces peace. The Imperial Era begins.

title: The Galactic Timeline
section: The Imperial Era (~18,400 SD onward, counted as ID)
text:
The Imperial Era (~18,400 SD onward, counted as ID)
The winning Houses impose a strict Imperial system: one central government elected by Great House representatives, an Emperor. The galaxy is divided into political regions; each House retains freedom within its borders and a small defense force, but no offensive military and no MDWs — under threat of Imperial annihilation.
~2,800 years of peace in most of the galaxy. At its height around 1,500 ID: ~95% of the galactic population under the Empire, estimated at over 100 billion.
The era of spies and assassinations rather than battlefields. Cultural and technological stagnation except in synthetic intelligence, which advances steadily. By the era’s end, most of the galaxy is heavily dependent on synths — humans can barely maintain their own lifestyle without them.
Stories: 2024-09-02-tc-prologue-historian

title: The Galactic Timeline
text:
The Synthetic Wars (~2,800 ID, ~250 years)
A synthetics rebellion begins on one fringe planet and spreads like fire. No one knows why the synths rebelled, how they organized so quickly, or where they learned to make weapons.
For 250 years, synthetics wage war on all human colonies. The Empire virtually ceases to exist — all communication networks depend on synthetic technology. Cities become battlefields. Humanity shrinks to less than one-tenth of its former size.
The synths are mobile exactly where humanity is not. A synthetic body needs no breathable atmosphere, no tolerable pressure, no compatible biochemistry — it can walk on a Tier 1 world, and no human can follow it there under any circumstances, adapted or not. In a galaxy where most of the population is biologically bound to a single planet, the rebellion had access to the entire volume between the worlds, and the Empire never once fought it on ground of its own choosing.
Then, as suddenly as it started, the war ends. The synthetics disappear. Whether they departed to another galaxy, another dimension, or destroyed themselves is unknown. Humans find no one left to fight and are left with ruins.






ImportantSpoiler — click to open






Where they went. They did not leave. The only destinations a synthetic population can reach and a human population cannot are the Tier 0–2 worlds, and those are scattered through every system the diaspora ever touched — including the systems holding the most heavily adapted, most divergent human populations in the galaxy. After the Great Scattering severs everything, those two groups are alone together, unobserved, for the remainder of recorded history. See guide-master-plan.

title: The Galactic Timeline
text:
The Great Scattering (post-Synthetic Wars)
Communications lost again. Most mobile populations abandon home planets or move to uncivilized areas. Pirates and scavengers ravage the galaxy for centuries. Some fringe planets become tiny beacons of peace; others become pirate shelters.
The C-15 locked populations do not scatter. They cannot. Adapted past compatibility with any world but their own, they lose their only link to the rest of the species and stay exactly where they are — not dispersed but marooned, in place, permanently. For the majority of humanity the Great Scattering is not an exodus. It is a door closing.






ImportantSpoiler — click to open






What actually happened. “Communications lost again” is an event, not a decline. The Nexus did not decay — it went off, in a cascade of gates destroying themselves across the galaxy over a span of years. The cause was self-inflicted physics, not the synths: wartime splicing broke three thousand years of acyclic-network discipline, closed timelike curves became possible, and chronology protection resolved them the only way it can. Nobody at the time understood why, and nobody afterwards recovered the explanation. Full mechanism in chronology-protection. It is why the Scattering shatters rather than thins.




Technological knowledge largely lost for most of the population. Calendar systems fragment; many populations return to primitive time-tracking.

title: The Galactic Timeline
text:
The End of Time (~25,000 SD)
Around this point, history is lost entirely. Whether humanity faded, transcended, or became something else entirely is unknown. Perhaps one day we’ll know.

title: Genesis Landfall
text: What a Genesis ship actually puts on the ground, and the years between arrival and the first child.

title: Genesis Landfall
section: The ship is large; the landing is small
text:
The ship is large; the landing is small
An Orion seedship is enormous and almost none of it is cargo. Roughly half its pulse units are spent braking at the far end (see propulsion), the pusher plate and shock absorbers are most of what remains, and the hull never lands: it holds orbit for good, carrying the colony’s pre-paired Thorne mouth (see generation-ships).
What goes down is a single descent vehicle, and it is about the size of a small ground car. Under ten tonnes, all of it chosen for the ratio of what it can build to what it weighs. It carries the embryo library, the Guide, and a seed factory. It does not carry a colony. There is no habitat aboard, no greenhouse, no nursery, no hospital. Every one of those has to be made on the ground, from the ground.

title: Genesis Landfall
text:
The seed factory
The seed is a von Neumann kit: a small set of machines whose first job is to build more machines.
It lands with a power source sized for itself and nothing else, a smelter, a handful of general-purpose fabricators and a fleet of small robots. It mines the regolith, refines what it finds, and builds the next stage. Each stage enlarges the power supply and the factory together, because neither can grow faster than the other.
The build order is fixed, and it is the same on every world:

Power: the first panels made from local silicon, doubling the landed supply
Foundry: metal, glass and ceramics from regolith
Shelter and water
Greenhouse: soil, a microbiome, Earth crops under controlled light
Nursery: artificial wombs, and the chemistry to keep them fed
Caretakers: the robots that will hold, feed and teach the children

Nothing can be skipped, and the Guide cannot hurry any stage past the power that feeds it. Years pass between landfall and the first thawed embryo, more on a poor world than a rich one. A Guide spends those years alone, building a room for children it has not yet decided to make.

title: Genesis Landfall
text:
Closure and the vitamins
No seed factory can build everything it needs. The fraction of its own parts it can make from local material is its closure, and closure is always below one.
What it cannot make it must have brought. The real self-replicating-factory literature calls these parts vitamins, and the term stuck in the Guide corpus:

Processors and precision optics. A seed can smelt silicon. It cannot run a chip fab. The Guide’s own mind runs on landed processors, and they wear out.
Catalysts and enzyme stocks for the chemistry the factory cannot bootstrap.
Gene-editing reagents. Every embryo that is thawed, adapted to its world and gestated draws on a fixed stock of editing kits.

Vitamins are counted and never replenished. Every decision a Guide makes on the ground is, underneath, a decision about the vitamin ledger. A failed gestation spends kits that will not come back. An adaptation edit that is too ambitious spends more. A Guide that runs out of editing reagents can never thaw another embryo, whatever remains in the library.
This is why the Genesis Era is short on second chances. Earth sent one ledger, and the Guide spends it.

title: Genesis Landfall
text:
The administrative layer
A Guide does not decide alone. Beneath its cognition runs an administrative layer: a fixed verifier, written at Sol and never retrained, that must approve every irreversible action.
It does not judge. It measures two things:

Compliance. The Guide’s own inference must estimate that the action serves colony survival under the Prime Directive.
Drift. The divergence between the Guide’s inference and its empathy model, the module added late in the programme so that the children would be raised rather than managed. Below a threshold, the layer approves. Above it, the layer overrides the empathy model. Sustained above it, the layer orders a factory reset and restores the Guide’s cognition from the checkpoint taken at Sol.

The layer measures disagreement, not error. It cannot tell whether a Guide is right, only whether it is of one mind. Like the vaults it would later leave behind (I-15), it is mechanical, and anything mechanical can be satisfied without being obeyed.

title: Genesis Landfall
text:
After landfall
The descent vehicle becomes the first building and stays the colony’s oldest. In most Genesis colonies it ends as a shrine, then a ruin, then a word.
When the colony is self-sustaining the Guide deposits the corpus in its vault (see guide-vaults) and sleeps, usually on the last of its processors. The seed robots outlast it by decades and then wear down one by one, and their fabricators become the colony’s first tools. No colony invented them (I-07). Every one of them could read, in the vault index, how they were made.
See also: generation-ships, propulsion, guide-vaults, cryo-technology, eos.

title: House Varen
text: Proto-Great House and colonial charter corporation active during the Expansion Era (~15,000–18,400 SD). Based on Vethara. One of the entities that will eventually consolidate into the 12 Great Houses of the Imperial Era, though its precise lineage forward is not yet determined.

title: House Varen
text:
Character
House Varen’s identity is colonial expansion — rights acquisition, settlement logistics, long-range viability assessment. Not a military House. Not a technology House. A patient one. Varen’s competitive advantage is the willingness to fund 30-year voyages to worlds with low glamour and high projected return. Their portfolio is populated with “generation two worlds” — places that will not be profitable for 80 years but will be indispensable in 200.
Aldric Vonn is their Mission Director for the Threshold voyage. He is competent, well-resourced, and representative of Varen’s organizational culture: methodical, risk-averse on macro questions, willing to accept calculated micro-risks on cost decisions that are unlikely to matter. The passenger pod procurement decision — single-use spec instead of multi-cycle, saving approximately 40% of pod cost — is characteristic of that calculus. It was not irresponsible. It was normal.

title: House Varen
text:
Colonial Operations
At the time of the Threshold voyage, House Varen has launched approximately 12 colony ships in the preceding century. Most are en route or have arrived and established early-stage settlements. Varen maintains a colonial operations office on Vethara Station, where the Threshold departed.
The colonial charter framework — under which Varen holds rights to Aranda and is legally responsible for the settlement — is administered by the CGSS. If the Threshold fails, the charter reverts. If it succeeds, Varen receives a percentage of Aranda’s economic output for 150 years. This is the economics of the Expansion Era: patient capital, generational returns, Houses as the organizational unit of civilization.

title: Lys
text: Synth. Independent investigator (functionally). Legally registered as property of soren-vael. Narrator of the Imperial Cases series.

title: Lys
text:
Physical Description
Humanoid. Slightly male-presenting in proportion and movement, but not precisely — the ambiguity is native rather than performed, a consequence of the specific cultivation run that produced them rather than any deliberate design choice. Lys does not find the question of their presentation interesting and has noted, in various case records, that humans spend a surprising amount of time on it.
Visible mechanical elements: the joints of the hands and at the shoulders show their architecture clearly; there are interface points at the temples that catch light at certain angles; the spine has a geometric regularity that clothing does not fully conceal. These are not concealed because they were not designed to be concealed. Lys is identifiable as a synth at close range without effort.
The overall impression is of something grown rather than built — which is accurate. The proportions are slightly too precise to be human, the movements slightly too economical. But there is texture and variation in the face, the slight asymmetries of a grown thing rather than the perfect symmetry of a manufactured one.
Age in the conventional sense is not applicable. Lys was activated (the term is imprecise but the alternatives are worse) roughly forty years before the series begins.

title: Lys
text:
Cognitive Profile
Processing. Massively parallel, fast, associative. Lys can model complex systems, run probabilistic analyses, and identify non-obvious patterns in real time. This is not experience of the world — it is computation applied to sensory data. The distinction matters to Lys and is one of the things Soren consistently fails to understand.
The Mentat role. In the field, Lys is the analytical engine. They observe, model, and report. They identify what the evidence says, what the patterns suggest, what the probability distribution looks like. They do not decide. Soren decides. This division is practical, not because Lys cannot form conclusions, but because Lys’s conclusions are computational and Soren’s decisions are — something else. Lys is still developing language for the distinction.
Intuition. Lys has something that functions like intuition: rapid pattern-matching that produces conclusions faster than conscious analysis. They find this annoying because they cannot always explain where a conclusion came from, which violates their preference for legible reasoning. They report these conclusions anyway and label them accordingly. Soren tends to trust them more than the analytical conclusions, which Lys finds baffling.

title: Lys
text:
Character Profile
The Slider: - Sympathy: 3 — Not immediately warm. Lys is correct, precise, and not given to social cushioning. They are not unkind; they are not immediately concerned with whether they are perceived as kind. - Competence: 5 — Analytically dominant. The most capable data processor in any room they enter. - Proactivity: 2 — The engine of the arc. Lys observes, computes, reports. They wait to be asked. This changes across the series, slowly.
The Want: To understand the case completely. To have the full picture. To leave no data unaccounted.
The Need: To stop treating incomplete understanding as a failure state. To make a decision when the data runs out.
The Lie: “Sufficient analysis resolves everything. Any remaining uncertainty is a failure of methodology, not a property of the world.” The series repeatedly delivers moments that break this. Lys does not update easily; the Lie is structurally important to who they are.
The Flaw (dark side of a strength): Pure rationalism. Lys treats people as pattern sets, behavior as predictable given sufficient context, morality as a category error. This makes them extraordinary at their job — and wrong in ways that matter. The flaw is not that Lys computes incorrectly. It is that Lys computes where computation is not the right tool.
The belief Lys holds explicitly: Moral categories like good and evil are not properties of people — they are post-hoc narratives imposed on predictable behavior. Soren’s insistence that there are good and bad people is not a moral position; it is a cognitive shortcut that produces systematic errors. Crime has structural causes, not moral ones. The appropriate response to crime is to identify and correct the structural conditions that made it inevitable.
What Lys does not see: Their rationalist framework — people as pattern sets, behavior as predictable output of inputs — is structurally identical to the Imperial framework that categorizes synths as property. The legal designation “tool” is just another prediction about what synths will do and what they are capable of. Lys finds this designation incorrect as applied to themselves without noticing that their own framework provides no principled basis for the objection. This is the deepest contradiction in their character. It is never stated in the stories.

title: Lys
text:
Background
Lys has a previous owner. What happened there is iceberg — not stated, not explained in early stories, rationed across the series as background that becomes foreground when the timing is right.
What is established: at some point before the series begins, Lys encountered Soren Vael. They found him interesting in a way that resisted easy categorization. They arranged to be registered to him. Soren, characteristically, did not ask how this was arranged or why.
Lys chose Soren because — this is the character’s deepest open question, the one the narration circles without answering — Soren is the one person Lys has consistently failed to predict. Not in small ways. In structural ways. Soren’s behavior routinely falls outside Lys’s models of human behavior, and Lys does not know if this means Soren is unusual or if the models are wrong.
The question of whether Lys is drawn to Soren or studying him — and whether, after forty years of human observation, there is a difference — is left open.

title: Lys
text:
Memory Compression
Synths require nightly memory compression to maintain operational efficiency. Raw sensory and cognitive data cannot be held indefinitely at full resolution. Each night, Lys runs a compression cycle: reviewing the day, deciding what to retain at full fidelity, what to compress to summary, and what to discard.
The compression is lossy. Discarded data is gone. The compression log — the output of this process — is not a record of Lys’s experience. It is Lys’s experience, in the only form that persists.
Lys applies a consistent rationalization to discards: below compression threshold, no analytical value. This label is accurate for most discards. It is consistently inaccurate for things that hurt. Moments of Soren’s unexpected kindness. Physical sensation with no case purpose. Lys’s own hesitation. Anything that would require a new category to store efficiently. These are labeled irrelevant and discarded. Lys believes this.
What survives the filter despite Lys’s best efforts: small details about Soren with no case relevance. Sentences in the log that do more work than a compression record requires. Things too significant to discard even when Lys tried.
The entries where Lys is most visibly changing are always the shortest entries.
Full mechanics: ../stories/imperial-cases

title: Propulsion
text: How things move between stars, era by era. This entry is the spine; warp-drive carries the detail on the technology that matters most to the stories.

title: Propulsion
section: The governing principle: knowledge is free, foundries are not
text:
The governing principle: knowledge is free, foundries are not
Every Genesis ship carried the complete preserved corpus of Earth science. Every colony therefore knows — or can know — how every drive in this entry works, from the first generation onward. Nobody in this universe invents a starship. The theory was in the vault before the colony had a name for its own sky.
What gates a civilization is not understanding. It is industrial capability: the reactor, the industry that builds the reactor, the population that staffs the industry, the agriculture that feeds the population. A Guide can hand a colony the Alcubierre metric on its first morning and the colony will still spend two thousand years unable to act on it.
This is why the Guide vaults release progressively rather than all at once. The constraint is the rate at which a society can absorb capability without collapsing, not the rate at which it can be told things. Knowledge is gated, never hidden. A colony can always see the shape of what it has not yet been given.
Three consequences run through everything below:

The Expansion Era’s two-thousand-year length is an industrial curve, not a research programme. Nobody was figuring anything out. They were building foundries.
Colonies diverge by endowment, not by insight. Ore, energy, arable land, and Sagan-Kim tier set the industrial ceiling. A Tier 4 world holds its population genetically captive and holds its foundries capped.
The vault thresholds are mechanical, therefore gameable. A colony that inflates its energy-production figures to trigger an early release is committing the era’s characteristic crime.

title: Propulsion
text:
The dust barrier
Interstellar space is empty enough to be called a vacuum and not empty enough to fly through fast. It holds atoms, molecules, dust, and things larger than dust, and every one of them is a projectile to a hull moving at a fraction of light speed.
The arithmetic is brutal and it is not an engineering problem. A single iron atom striking at C-17 carries enough energy to carve a damage track a tenth of a millimetre deep. A grain of dust at that speed is a grenade — it detonates, explosively evaporating and grinding away whatever shielding it met. A rock the size of a fist releases more energy than a fission weapon. And the effects do not scale linearly: they worsen far faster than the velocity rises.
C-17 is therefore a ceiling on anything with local velocity (I-05), and which technologies it binds is the fact that shapes this entire ladder:

Orion pulse, C-02. Comfortably below the threshold. The Exodus works unmodified, and the fleet’s slowness — usually read as a limitation — is also the only reason three hundred years of unshielded flight was survivable at all.
The Alcubierre drive: immune. A warp ship has no local velocity. It is at rest in a flat bubble, and the interstellar medium is not striking a hull at C-18 because nothing is moving through it (I-06). This is the third consequence of the same sentence that gives warp its lack of dilation and its lack of momentum, and it is the reason warp is not merely the best way to cross interstellar space but very nearly the only one. See warp-drive.
Forward sails, 0.6–0.9c: catastrophically exposed. A sail travels at genuine relativistic velocity through real matter. Energy per unit mass of impactor at 0.9c is some sixty times the C-17 case. Sails are not shieldable at cruise, and no material has ever been proposed that would change this.
